If you’re interested in becoming any level of organizer for EWOC, this course is mandatory. If you can’t make all of the sessions, reach out to san-francisco@workerorganizing.org for accommodations. RSVP here Hands Off Our Vote! DSA SF joins other organizations in the Bay Resistance coalition to support an election defense resolution that will introduced by Supervisor Chyanne Chen at the San Francisco Board of Supervisors this Tuesday. This resolution asks that San Francisco commit to protecting election integrity, oppose interference in the election and voter intimidation, and that San Franciscans have the right to exercise their constitutional rights of freedom of speech and right to assemble to defend free and democratic elections. Organizations that have signed onto this resolution include Bay Resistance, SF Rising, the San Francisco Labor Council, the California Nurses Association, SEIU USWW, the California Federation of Teachers, Indivisible SF, just to name a few. A 9:30 AM press conference is scheduled to take place this Tuesday at SF City Hall to announce the resolution. We need to be ready to stand up to Trump and MAGA should they cause election chaos and try to delegitimize the election results.

articles.title: Financial Capital Didn’t Make New York City Great
articles.author: Daniel Wortel-London
articles.content: It’s the beginning of the new Ric Burns documentary on New York City, and Adam Gopnik is choking up. He’s talking about the diversity and tolerance that New York, at its best, embodies. He’s talking about the challenges the city has faced over the past fifty years. Above all, he’s talking about how it met those challenges: through its willingness to adapt. Cities are “self-emergent” and “self-sustaining” forms, Gopnik argues, but self-sustaining requires transformation. Happily, New York has been up to the task. “We accept [New York’s] remaking of itself again and again,” he avers, and it is this tradition of demographic and developmental pluralism (“plural pluralisms,” in his inimitable phrasing) that allowed Gotham to transcend its postwar decay and become the beacon of cosmopolitan, progressive liberalism we adore today. It’s a powerful way to open. It’s a message that many other bards of Gotham, from Walt Whitman and Jane Jacobs to Richard Sennett and Teju Cole, have proclaimed. But it’s a message almost entirely undercut by the structure and argument of the documentary that follows. That’s because, in the two latest episodes of Ric Burns’s long-running series New York — whose first five episodes aired in 1999, with two following in 2001 and another installment in 2003 — postwar Gotham is not saved by its “self-emergent” forms or the bottom-up moxie of its existing population but instead by the top-down, outside-in forces of globalization and capitalist development. In 1961, Jane Jacobs wrote that “cities have the capability of providing something for everybody, only because, and only when, they are created by everybody.” The New York City shown here is, for the most part, created by everybody except the ordinary people who live there. To be fair, in an interview about the documentary for the Hollywood Reporter , Burns called “capitalism and democracy and globalization” the “three great pieces of uranium in the city’s engine.” But democracy plays a minor role in this tale. We do not see, as in the series’ original episodes, how unions and tenant organizers struggled to bring Gotham’s economy under greater popular control. Nor do we hear from left-wing scholars like the late Marshall Berman and Mike Wallace who, in previous installments, added a grain of skepticism to the self-congratulating narratives spun by the city’s power brokers. Instead, we hear the story of Gotham’s redemption since the 1970s as the long, lonely struggle to make the city safe for globalized capitalism — accompanied, of course, by sweeping pans and saccharine Irish reels. This is not to say that ordinary New Yorkers are absent from this story. To the contrary: the documentary admirably recounts the patterns of cultural and social transformations that have coursed through the city over the past fifty years. But such pluralism, and the city’s broader liberal political culture, is framed here as dependent on the city’s successful courting of globalized capital since the 1970s — whereas the truth is that globalized capital in its current form now threatens those very virtues that New Yorkers hold dear. Fall and Rise? Every redemption arc requires a fall, and the first episode locates New York City’s fall in its postwar deindustrialization. We hear in admirably clear terms how the loss of manufacturing threatened both the city’s fiscal health and its heavily unionized, heavily working-class population. But the film blames deindustrialization on the impersonal, irresistible forces of “globalization” to which Gotham could either adapt or, in the narrator’s portentous words, “plummet into the widening abyss opening up between the past and the future.” This rhetoric, with its Clintonesque intonations of globalized inevitability, distorts the past. Historian Kenneth Jackson claims in the film that “the city tried to preserve those industrial districts.” Yet Joshua Freeman , a better-informed source on this point, writes in Working-Class New York that the city’s postwar leaders were “sanguine” about the flight of industrial jobs. Well before the mayoralty of Michael Bloomberg and his whiz kids, city leaders and bodies like the Regional Plan Association believed that New York needed to displace manufacturing in favor of globally oriented information and financial service industries. The series itself once said as much: in its earlier episode on the World Trade Center, historian Mike Wallace narrated how “monopoly capitalists” (his words) used public subsidies, zoning reforms, and other tools to “expand the financial core” of downtown at the expense of working-class manufacturing jobs. This process of financialization did not follow the loss of manufacturing; financialization accompanied and accelerated that loss. Why does this matter? The documentary attributes the city’s fiscal crisis of the 1970s to the “inevitable” loss of the city’s manufacturing tax base. But if the city had already begun pivoting toward a financial services economy by that point, then not only was the fiscal crisis exacerbated by local choices: it means also that the city’s financial service economy might have contributed to the crisis. This was precisely what many activists argued at the time. “A city can’t let its skills, manufacturing plants and suppliers’ plants wither away and then not suffer the consequences,” Jane Jacobs complained in 1975. “The notion that the city could live on financial and white-collar services was nonsense.” Corporate expansion, she and others argued, added to the city’s debt and undercut well-paying entry-level jobs, which in turn swelled the city’s costly welfare state. But to give airtime to this argument would interfere with the documentary’s core message: that adapting to globalized finance was necessary if New York was to survive its crisis. There was no alternative. Every adaptation comes with challenges, however. Coming out of the fiscal crisis, New York tells us, Gotham surrendered “fiscal control of its affairs to a small board of bankers and businessmen.” This refreshingly blunt language is paired with equally welcome commentary from political scientist Ester Fuchs, who traces the subsequent decay of public services and rise in crime to the austerity this board unleashed. But, as happens so often in the film, the acknowledgment of pain is accompanied by hedging (“some believed,” “perhaps”) and a countervailing claim: in this case, that the austerity plan devised by the control board, whatever its short-term effects, was a “long-term blueprint for stabilizing the city’s finances.” But the plan, as historians like Kim Phillips-Fein have documented, was far more than a measure of fiscal relief. It was an effort to dismantle a particular model of politics, one in which the economy was embedded in, and subordinate to, democracy. The fiscal crisis was both the beginning and the exemplar of that dismantling. The documentary elides this fact, leaving us to assume that the city’s precrisis “liberal values” survived and even thrived thanks to the wisdom of the bankers’ junta. But the bankers knew better. The “pressing need” regarding the city’s welfare state, a Salomon Brothers investment guide stated in 1975, was not to “finance it” but “to change it.” And that is exactly what they did. Rather than see New York City’s post-1970s story as one of redemption and transcendence, it is equally accurate to see it in terms of profound loss. But that would make for a very different documentary. Ordinary New Yorkers are included in the narrative, to be sure. The film covers the postwar migration of black and Latino New Yorkers, the segregation that confined them, and the cultures they created. We hear about the movements of the 1960s: gay rights, black power, student power, women’s liberation. We hear how immigrants arriving after the Hart-Celler Act of 1965 helped stabilize and revitalize city neighborhoods during the dark days of the 1970s. But here too, the argument about their role is ambivalent. Fuchs may declare that immigrant transformation “at the neighborhood level . . . is as important as bringing in the big fish on the economic side of things.” But this is somewhat offset by another commentator’s claim that “Wall Street single-handedly revived New York.” Beyond Wall Street and immigration, the documentary credits the city’s revival to its leaders’ success in reducing crime in the 1980s and ’90s. This reduction deserves celebration: no one who watches the footage recovered here will forget how violence and the fear of violence degrades the public realm. But the documentary is equally revealing when it links the city’s corporate reconstruction to the development of its local police state. As New York University Professor Mitchell Moss puts it, “what Bloomberg did with finance,” Deputy Commissioner Jack Maple “did . . . with crime.” The film even recounts Maple scribbling his new policing strategy (“rapid deployment, effective tactics, relentless follow-up”) on a cocktail napkin at Elaine’s as if he were founding a new start-up. This convergence of neoliberal technocracy with law-and-order conservatism, arguably the story of America’s post-1970s political economy, is addressed with some vigor by Ric’s brother Ken in his documentary on the Central Park jogger travesty. But while Ric does not shy away from examining police brutality under Rudy Giuliani, the broader tensions between the establishment of a militarized NYPD state-within-a-state and the pluralistic pretensions of liberal Gotham are underexplored. Enter Bloomberg The second episode, covering the city since 2001, works hard to convince us that these two decades were the “most challenging . . . in the city’s entire history.” Terrorism, climate change, and a global pandemic called into question not only New York’s future, we are told, but “the future of cities” itself. And the documentary would also have us believe the city survived thanks less to the “thousand small sanities” of Gopnik’s liberal imagination than to the very large sanity of one man: Michael Bloomberg, mayor from 2002 to 2013 and, in one commentator’s words, “the greatest mayor in New York City history.” For more than an hour the film lavishes attention on the three-termer’s “scientific” approach to counterterrorism, the rebuilding of Ground Zero, the residential remaking of the waterfront, and other accomplishments. Having lived in New York through those years, I can vouch for Bloomberg’s administrative efficacy. I, too, appreciate the High Line and The Gates , the bike lanes and 311. But it would have been nice, amid the interviews with admiring aides and acolytes, to hear from a few of the activists and advocates who disagreed with him. What would tenant organizers say to the claim that the city’s rezonings were “gradual” and touched only vacant manufacturing land? What would Asad Dandia, the borough historian of Brooklyn who was himself surveilled by an NYPD informant as a college student, say about the department’s claim to have “foiled sixteen terrorist attacks” thanks to their derring-do? Above all, what would Bloomberg’s critics say about his effort to rebrand New York as a “luxury city”? We do hear about the city’s “astounding” inequality during and after his tenure, about its link to Wall Street’s growth, even about its “spiritually corrupting” effects. But we do not hear about these outcomes as deliberate local policy choices. Indeed, the film makes the conventional Manhattan Institute claim that the city offers the poor more opportunity than elsewhere in America “in part, at least,” because of its inequality. Now, New York is certainly a bright spot in the US economy. But to read that as a verdict on the city’s capacity for innovation, or on the health of cities generally, is backward. New York long ago chose the route of becoming the nation’s rentier, the Empire City to which the periphery paid tribute through the interest, dividends, and land rents directed toward Gotham’s financial sector. And the divergent fortunes of New York and a handful of metros on one side, and struggling cities and “left behind” regions on the other, do not herald “the future of cities.” They suggest a future where urbanity has become a luxury in distinction from and at the expense of formerly vibrant urban centers. But this is not how the documentary understands urban crises. Thus, Zohran Mamdani’s election is framed as a referendum on Eric Adams’s “sell-out” to Donald Trump and Immigration and Customs Enforcement, a matter of attitudes toward immigration more than affordability. As the narrator recounts, “It was perhaps for that reason [the sell-out], in part, that in the fall of 2025 . . . New Yorkers went to the polls and, for the first time in the city’s history, sent a Muslim mayor to city hall, perhaps wishing to show that even in the hardest of times, the city’s commitment to providing a home for all the peoples of the world remained unwavering.” Zohran is indeed striving to provide a home for all the peoples of the world. But he also wants to help preserve New York as a home for all New Yorkers: to preserve the city as a place of diversity where ordinary working-class people can afford to live. The change-besotted documentary, of course, makes preservation and pluralism seem like contradictions in terms. But Mamdani, and New York voters, seem to know better. Which Way, New York? In the series’ earlier episode on the World Trade Center, historian Niall Ferguson offered an interesting reading of the September 11 attacks. Where others framed them purely as an assault on liberal democracy (“they hate us for our freedom”), Ferguson argued that the towers’ advocates “thought they could have the benefits of a globalized economy and none of the costs. They thought you could globalize economics but not politics, not violence.” And he was right. Something similar, I suspect, is true today. The would-be defenders of New York point to its diversity and tolerance, its cultural breadth and civic spirit, as the great fruits of globalized capitalism. Those who resent New York from the benighted “left behind” regions, unable to pivot as Gotham did, simply resent our success and way of life. They hate us for our freedom. But just as globalized capitalism helped push the city into fiscal crisis, it has played no small part in creating the forces now in revolt against it and the liberalism it represents. Its financial sector helped destabilize and drain the economic life from entire regions in the United States; it worked to enrich Trump; above all, the affordability crisis it has driven and benefits from is threatening the very social, cultural, and intellectual diversity that once made New York great. Indeed, we might see the overconcentration of financialized economic activity in New York and the decline of opportunity in many other places as two faces of a single crisis of liberal pluralism. Some will say, as Ric Burns’s documentary does over and over, that we’ve seen all this before: that globalization and capitalism are constants in Gotham’s history. Yet there are alternatives to the path of economic development the city has chosen. And if plutocratic conditions within New York cannot preserve the values of liberalism and pluralism we most value about it, perhaps their preservation will have to come from outside it through an evening out of our nation’s economic geography, as advocated by Lewis Mumford; or as another illustrious thinker once put it, through “ the abolition of the antithesis between town and country .” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Focus on the Real Drivers of the Affordability Crisis
articles.author: Robbie Nelson
articles.content: Over the past five years, the price of consumer goods has dominated American political discourse. From Donald Trump to Zohran Mamdani, winning candidates have used “affordability politics” to articulate popular dissatisfaction with economic conditions. From the price of eggs to gas to burritos, the terms of discussion in the media, the campaign trail, and the proverbial kitchen table have revolved around the cost-of-living crisis embodied in these consumer goods. Although figures on the Right and center of the political scene have used inflation and affordability politics to bolster their agendas, during the second Trump administration, it is the Left and center left that have principally benefited from the salience of price talk. Indeed, the Democrats’ 2026 midterm messaging strategy has centered on blaming Trump’s Republicans for the cost-of-living crisis that Trump himself successfully pinned on Joe Biden just two years ago. That aggressive focus on the cost of living and a promise of consumer affordability will likely continue to be a successful playbook for both left and right anti-incumbent campaigns in the coming years. But in order for a political movement to actually address the cost-of-living crisis once in office, it needs a clearer picture of where those costs are coming from and how they have changed over time. Our affordability politics must go beyond lowering the price of eggs. And trends in American household spending underscore perhaps the central task of the Left: expanding the welfare state with universal, solidaristic, and visible social programs. Where Do Americans Spend Their Money? Anyone purchasing gas, groceries, cars, or airline tickets in the 2020s has experienced sticker shock since the onset of inflationary pressures catalyzed by COVID-19, tariffs, the artificial intelligence bubble, and the disastrous wars in Ukraine and Iran. But a longer view reveals a different picture. Compared to forty years ago, Americans today spend less of their total disposable income on food, transportation, clothing, and personal care. And they spend significantly more than they used to on health care, education, housing, and financial products (retirement contributions, nonmedical insurance, etc.). While we can see a modest rise in food and transportation budget shares from 2020–24, it does little to change the overall trends. When we look specifically at households with children, an even more dramatic story comes to the fore, in which the ballooning costs of education and childcare have nearly tripled their share of household spending. The roots of these contradictory dynamics lay in the neoliberal class compromise of the late 1970s, which resulted in lower prices for consumer goods but much higher prices for the assets and services that sustain social reproduction. After the labor and popular upsurges of the 1960s and ’70s were defeated, the weakened American working class accepted job cuts due to automation and offshoring, and the more vulnerable among domestic producers were forced to accept a new free trade regime that opened them up to global competition. While wages were lower, jobs more precarious, and employee benefits like pensions and health insurance increasingly scant, workers and their families could purchase food, clothing, electronics, and consumer durables (appliances, furniture, automobiles, etc.) at lower prices. The shift of world garment production to the Global South during the globalization waves of the 1980s–2000s has driven down US household budget allocations for apparel by a whopping 60 percent. The declines are more modest but still meaningful (roughly 15 percent) in food and transportation. Again, these price changes are linked to the globalization of supply chains in the food, automobile, and energy sectors. As this process unfolded, American workers and households were also increasingly forced to bear the monetary costs of their own social reproduction. Postindustrial developments in the US economy reinforced changing cultural mores to spur shifts in family and education. The end of the “breadwinner wage” and greater gender freedoms meant more women in the paid workforce, fewer households with parents acting as full-time caregivers, and greater numbers of people funneled into higher education to prepare for the medical, education, and knowledge economy careers that required such credentials. Millions more Americans were paying for education, from daycare to graduate school. And the costs of that education kept rising. Over this same period, the US health care system experienced a weakening of employer-based health coverage for unionized workers, and increasingly powerful and consolidated insurance, medical device, hospital, and pharmaceutical corporations. These dynamics, along with longer lifespans, have driven astronomical rises in costs across the board. With the partial exception of Obamacare’s expansion of Medicaid — which was limited in red states by the reactionary Supreme Court — any federal attempts to bring down out-of-pocket health care costs have been thin gruel. It is worth pausing here to reflect on an interesting paradox: in 1984, when US residents spent a much lower percentage of their household budgets on health care, the United States placed much higher in global rankings of health . Educational quality is more difficult to compare internationally, but it’s clear that drastically higher household expenditure on education has not propelled the United States to the top of global rankings . Since the 1980s, Americans have increasingly purchased services of social reproduction through market mechanisms — paid childcare, university education, privately bought insurance, out-of-pocket health care costs, elder care, 401(k) contributions — relying less and less on things like unpaid gendered household labor, collectively bargained health care benefits, defined benefit pensions, and free or cheap higher education. The marketization of social reproduction, combined with runaway cost spirals in education and especially health care, has fundamentally reshaped the budget priorities for average US households. The rise of health care, education, and retirement saving costs is the dramatic story. Housing, perhaps surprisingly, has stayed relatively stable, its share of household expenditure rising only 3 percentage points between 1984 and 2024. But unsurprisingly, it remains the largest single item in US household budgets. Comprising roughly a third of average household expenditures, the cost of shelter is the single largest drain on American bank accounts. The high and rising cost of housing in metropolitan areas has been a key driver of left-wing political success in major US cities, with Zohran Mamdani’s campaign emblematic of this phenomenon. The residential real estate market is incredibly complex, with drastic regional and subregional differences, so there won’t be a one-size-fits-all approach to addressing this issue. But the basic playbook pursued by the Mamdani administration — strengthening rent stabilization, cutting unnecessary red tape to aid more construction, repairing and building more social housing where possible — is a good start at the local level. We desperately need more federal funding and support for affordable and social housing, especially given the fiscal constraints that states and municipalities face. But in general, the complexity and diversity of the American housing market makes it unsuitable as a centerpiece of national policy and messaging for the Left. For starters, a majority in the country are homeowners and thus at least partially benefit from rising prices. Furthermore, while expensive metro areas have seen huge rises in housing costs, the dynamic is different in much of the country. Nationwide, housing as a percentage of household expenditures rose from around 30 percent in 1984 to 33 percent in 2024. But in the New York City metropolitan area, that number is over 38 percent. The wide variations in housing expenditures as a percentage of household budgets between and within regions makes it categorically different from other expenditures whose regional discrepancies are minimal. Housing costs are clearly a major issue across American society. But the most drastic structural changes in household expenditures over the past decades are found in education, health care, and retirement contributions. How Do Cost-Of-Living Politics Work? If the data clearly shows that food, transportation, and consumer durables have declined in their significance to American household spending, then why do the prices of those items maintain their centrality to cost-of-living discourse in this country? In a structural sense, politicizing the price of consumer goods makes sense, because people tend to purchase those items frequently, and their prices are displayed in a visible and public fashion. In the case of gasoline, large signs showing its price are a key visual feature of the American landscape. It makes sense that people feel comfortable discussing the price of goods whose prices have — by virtue of public signage in grocery stores, restaurants, car dealerships, gas stations, and media advertisements — already been introduced into the available public lexicon. Across the country, the price of gas ranks just below the weather as universally accessible small-talk fodder. By contrast, the cost of a medical procedure — along with the complex constellation of premiums, deductibles, and co-pays that structure the price of health care — is opaque and private. Not only are those bills sent directly and privately, the actual costs are rendered purposefully opaque, even to the intended recipient. Ditto for educational costs, where a Rube Goldberg–esque system of scholarships, loans, vouchers, tax credits, financial aid, not to mention “indirect” education costs like lodging, materials, and food all conspire to make the published price of an educational experience frustratingly incomplete. The public/private dynamic at play in price information is reinforced, or perhaps driven, by the social and cultural distinctions between the “public” life of market activity and the “private” life of things like health and family. While people’s increasing willingness to speak publicly about the cost of things like daycare, eldercare, and hospital stays is a positive development, in general, most people would be much more comfortable complaining about the price of their Chipotle burrito than their colonoscopy or mental health counseling. Some liberals have leaned on pop psychology to understand inflation politics. Economist Justin Wolfers wrote condescendingly in T he New York Times that normal people are too irrational and emotional to understand the economics of inflation and concluded that a psychological trick of timing creates false anger at the economy. In this telling, you first get a raise, but then that gain feels snatched away by higher prices. While the consumer ends up affording the same amount of goods, it feels like theft because of the timing and sequencing. By the end of that piece, however, Wolfers does manage to put his finger on something meaningful: people are particularly upset about prices right now, because Trump campaigned on lower prices, then implemented policies (tariffs, wars, AI bubble inflation) that raised prices. By historicizing the political psychology of inflation, we get closer to real insight. Most Americans understand, at least implicitly, the terms of the class settlement that produced the post-1980s economic order. In exchange for degraded pay and working conditions, workers in the postindustrial West gained access to the cheap, plentiful, on-demand goods that were the fruits of Global South–based supply chains. It wasn’t a great deal from the vantage point of the average American — not to mention the ecological devastation and the expanded regimes of labor exploitation in the Global South — but Western populations did receive tangible benefits in the form of cheaper consumer goods. When the terms of this social-economic contract were disrupted by the global supply chain shocks first of COVID-19, then of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and also the electronics and energy demand suck of the AI bubble, people reacted poorly. If working people can’t even keep the thin consumer benefits of our capital-dominated social contract, then what’s the point of this whole charade? Capitalism’s global hegemony is by no means waning, but the potency of “cost-of-living” discourse across the world reveals a depth of a social feeling that the expected benefits of capitalist growth are not matching expectations. That social feeling can be a resource for renewed socialist and working-class politics, but we needn’t accept all the premises of already-existing affordability politics to draw on it. From Affordability to Decommodification A socialist response to the cost-of-living crisis can be, on paper, pretty straightforward. First and foremost, avoid the Biden administration communications strategy of insisting that “the economy is great, actually.” Instead of waving away people’s anxieties about inflation in the cost of basic goods with statistics, we should instead reinforce the chorus of anger about rising costs for daily necessities. But we should also avoid the 2024 Trump campaign’s preferred strategy of focusing on particular consumer goods (like beef, eggs, or gasoline) and promising to bring their particular prices down. Instead, shift the political conversation toward our home turf: empowering workers and unions, raising the minimum wage, and most of all, expanding the welfare state. Decommodifying the services necessary for social reproduction is a popular and viable political program that actually would make the greatest progress toward addressing people’s ability to afford their lives. To be politically sustainable, these programs must be designed to be visible, universal , and generous. In other words, we must expand the welfare state in ways that are neither means-tested nor disguised through tax credits. The recent re-reemergence of Medicare for All as a legislative priority for progressives and socialists speaks to these logics. Not only would a single-payer health care system improve health outcomes, boost social solidarity, and decrease economic and social precarity; it would address a major vector driving the cost-of-living crisis. Demands for tuition-free higher education, trade school, and early childhood care form another core plank in this version of an affordability agenda. Although less universal than health care (not everybody has children, or enrolls in postsecondary education), the benefits will be life-changing for those eligible. On the retirement front, removing the income cap for Social Security and embedding more robust cost-of-living increases would make the system solvent and ensure that the system is more than a threadbare safety net. One can already hear the rising chorus of centrist and conservative pundits: “How are you going to pay for it?” While the full answer contains complexity and nuance, the short answer is and has always been “raising taxes.” And while progressive taxation is essential for structuring the welfare state, sustainable social programs require broad revenue bases across all sectors of society. As the late Marxist economist Anwar Shaikh showed , it was the working class that, historically speaking, largely funded its own welfare state. While short-term political considerations push left-wing politicians to target new taxes toward billionaires and pied-à-terre owners, we need to be laying foundations for a longer-term program of tax raises. We cannot dissemble our way to a solidaristic welfare state but need to make the case openly that implementing Medicare for All would require raising most people’s taxes; for the vast majority of taxpayers, the abolition of out-of-pocket costs would more than make up for the increased rates. And beyond the dollars and cents, the peace of mind and freedom that comes with delinking health care from employment would be a liberatory experience for tens of millions. The insistence on lowering the prices for specific consumer goods also runs into a longer-term problem. While sharp price hikes in recent years can, in many cases, be blamed on corporate price gouging and “greedflation,” supply chain bottlenecks, and disastrous foreign policy decisions, the baseline of super-low prices for food, transportation, and consumer durables is dependent on the exploitation of workers in the Global South, environmental devastation, and expectations of product disposability. A political program that empowers workers in both the Global North and the Global South (while still remaining, for now, under capitalism) will raise the cost of most consumer goods. We should remove or mitigate the large structural costs of social reproduction that weigh most heavily on household budgets and give ourselves more room to pay more for consumer goods. If we want to give future political projects a fighting chance for a healthier, less exploitative, and more solidaristic world, we need to start laying the political and discursive groundwork now. Decommodifying systems of social reproduction remains the most urgent and potentially transformative task of a Left that wins any sort of legislative power in a postindustrial democracy. Zohran Mamdani’s initial virality was fueled in part by pushing for lower prices at halal carts and creating public grocery stores, but his legacy will ultimately rest on his success in delivering on promises like universal childcare and freezing the rent. articles.title: Alberta’s Post-Referendum Hangover
articles.author: Laurence Miall
articles.content: Alberta is one of the unhappiest provinces in Canada, a reminder of the old adage that money can’t buy happiness. The province fails to responsibly manage the riches from its oil and gas sector, leaving little of the spoils to Alberta workers, while billions in profits flow to foreign shareholders, many of them American. Perhaps the unhappiest of all Albertans are the separatists. This right-wing populist fringe helped push the province into a deeply divisive referendum, which failed in its aim to garner support for independence from Canada. The October 19 referendum’s very existence suggests that Premier Danielle Smith is governing with an almost exclusive focus on managing pressures within her party to protect her own leadership. Polling shows that support for independence has rarely exceeded 30 percent . And yet getting Alberta out of Canada has robust support within the premier’s own United Conservative Party (UCP). One of the most reputable pollsters in the province, Janet Brown, found earlier this fall that a majority of UCP voters, 53 percent, backed beginning the process toward a separation vote in the October referendum. In winning the UCP leadership in 2022, Danielle Smith was able to recruit new members with “little to no history of party politics,” drawn to her promise to push for more sovereignty for the province. She emerged as the anti-Ottawa candidate during Justin Trudeau’s increasingly unpopular tenure as prime minister. She also benefited from the strong pandemic-era anti-vaccine sentiment that helped bring down her predecessor, Jason Kenney. Smith promised that, under her leadership, Alberta would reject federal laws or court decisions that were deemed to be against the province’s interests. Go-Go Mandate Overreach Having secured the party’s leadership, Smith tacked toward safer political territory to successfully beat the center-left New Democratic Party (NDP) in the province’s 2023 election. Aware of the political sensitivity of universal public health care, she committed to a guarantee as the campaign approached: “Under no circumstances will any Albertan ever have to pay out of pocket for access to their family doctor or to get the medical treatment that they need.” Perhaps even more important than what Smith said was what she left unsaid. She did not campaign to suppress Alberta’s vibrant wind and solar energy industry, but after her election victory she announced a moratorium on new renewable electricity projects, in a move that appeared to come from nowhere. Nor did she campaign on invoking the unpopular notwithstanding clause four times in order to shield legislation from Charter challenges. Of those four invocations, the clearest violation of Charter rights was the law ordering striking teachers back to work — running roughshod over their Charter-protected right to strike. Finally, Smith most certainly did not campaign on holding a referendum on whether to begin the process toward a future vote on independence for Alberta. Arguably, Smith came to power by promising one thing to separatists and something quite different to the general voting public. In the spring of 2025, Albertan’s top priorities were health care, the cost of living, education, and affordable housing, according to a Nanos survey. These same broad concerns remained the leading issues in a Leger’s October 2025 poll . Yet in the post-referendum hangover, the concerns of working Albertans are again being ignored, and Albertans are likely to spend most of the rest of 2026 having to witness pointless bickering on the Right. This bickering started within hours of the “Remain” side having bested the separatists by 75 percent to 25 percent. Jeffrey Rath, one of the most prominent separatist organizers, characterized Smith’s federalist stance during the referendum campaign as a betrayal of the UCP party members who had supported her. He confirmed that he would push to remove her, “in the same way that we worked to get rid of Kenney.” He also alleged that Smith’s 2022 leadership campaign purchased the voter list of Wexit Canada, now the Maverick Party, and used it to pitch her as a “secret separatist.” A group of UCP constituency associations is pushing for an early review of Smith’s leadership. And in another sign of the turbulence that is the new daily reality for the governing party, a rural UCP representative, Shane Getson, abruptly announced his resignation on October 26. The referendum has exposed a deep divide within the UCP between separatists and federalists. There is no knowing how the battle for the party’s future will play out. Working families are hapless bystanders in what amounts to a political hostage situation. Tyranny of the Minority Professor Jared Wesley suggests that Albertans are not as divided nor as beholden to right-wing ideology as the mainstream media narrative asserts. He argues that the UCP presents itself as the “authentic voice of ‘ordinary people.’” The Alberta referendum, meanwhile, demonstrated how much influence the extremist fringe that helped elect Premier Smith had within the party: Smith called a vote on starting a process toward separation in spite of the fact that roughly two-thirds of voters rejected the option. As Wesley’s research has shown, a huge number of Albertans call themselves moderate. Add up the number of self-identified moderates, liberals, centrists, progressives, and socialists, and the resulting group would outnumber conservatives. These people are not well served by Premier Smith. Take the campaign promise that no Albertan would have to pay out of pocket to see a family doctor or receive needed medical treatment. This promise was quickly broken. In December 2025, Alberta passed the Health Statutes Amendment Act, which helped to establish what has been called by Friends of Medicare a two-tier health care system, allowing physicians to work in both the public and private system concurrently. This is a dangerous erosion of the principles of universality and a violation of the Canada Health Act. During a cost-of-living crisis, why should anyone pay for health care services that should be available through the public system? Or consider the unprecedented interference by the UCP in the renewable-energy industry. The Pembina Institute, an energy think tank, says that nearly eleven gigawatts of proposed wind, solar, and storage projects have been withdrawn from the province’s development waiting list, warning that the greater reliance on natural gas generation is likely to drive up electricity prices. Again and again, the UCP has opted to shore up support among separatist zealots and pro-fossil-fuel constituencies against the interests of ordinary working Albertans. Working-Class Politics for the Win What, then, is to be done? Despite the upheaval of Premier Smith’s tenure, recent polling still puts the UCP at a virtual dead heat with the NDP. Meanwhile, the government has set up a new electoral-boundaries review process overseen by a UCP-majority committee. Critics, including the NDP, have accused the UCP of attempting to gerrymander Alberta’s electoral map in its favor. The NDP should confront the UCP’s populism with a politics that puts working people ahead of elites and separatist hard-liners. This will involve making some bold policy choices. It might mean, for example, calling for a windfall profits tax on oil and gas revenues, and full public auto insurance. The party should take a serious look at the “ Worker Agenda ” proposed by the Alberta Federation of Labour and borrow the policy proposals that would be most viable in an election. Three-quarters of voters rejected starting a process toward separation. The citizenship and immigration questions won only narrow majorities; all four constitutional proposals failed . Now Alberta needs a revived NDP with a platform that unabashedly champions working-class people — and offers a genuine alternative to an out-of-touch UCP. articles.title: Is Ecuador Still a Democracy?
articles.author: Carlo Campo
articles.content: “I’d be lying to you if I told you that yesterday I didn’t double-lock the door, just in case they come to take us down in the middle of the night.” Those were the words of Jahiren Noriega, a member of Ecuador’s National Assembly, the day after the detention of Luisa González, the Movimiento Revolución Ciudadana’s presidential candidate in the country’s last two federal elections and the main opposition figure today. In Ecuador, where the separation of powers no longer exists, the use of lawfare by the far-right government of President Daniel Noboa blurs the line between democracy and dictatorship. For members of the Movimiento Revolución Ciudadana, the party aligned with the former socialist president, Rafael Correa, the political persecution is nothing new, and left-wing leaders and social movements across Latin America will surely recognize the playbook. But González’s detention last Thursday marks a shocking escalation in Noboa’s bold use of the courts to persecute opponents, and in Ecuador, a country with a rich history of protest that has been unusually quiet throughout his presidency, the Left faces its biggest test yet. Bogus Corruption Charges González was detained for alleged irregularities in the campaign financing of her presidential run in 2023. The case is being referred to as the Caso Laberinto — what the government describes as a labyrinth of money laundering. But it is more accurately the reopening of a previous case, the Caso Caja Chica, that was already adjudicated. That case was closed when Noboa’s government failed to prove its laughable accusation that González’s campaign contributions were linked to the Cartel de Los Soles, a group whose very existence is questioned , and it resulted in nothing more than a fine that was paid to the Tribunal Contencioso Electoral, the specialized body that administers electoral justice in Ecuador. Having failed to draw a line between González and a group that might not even exist, the public prosecutor’s office is now shamelessly claiming that the courts were wrong the first time: money laundering did indeed occur, and Aquiles Álvarez, the mayor of Guayaquil, Ecuador’s largest city, is involved. Also a member of the Revolución Ciudadana, Álvarez was detained in February in the Caso Goleada, a farcical case in which he was accused of building a business structure to illegally generate profits. He remains imprisoned. The reaction to González’s detention was immediate. Correa, who lives in self-imposed exile and was granted asylum in Belgium, was among the first to comment, saying : “In Ecuador, there exists a true dictatorship. It doesn’t respect the constitution, human rights.” He pointed out the timing of the arrest, as Ecuadorians will head to the polls in November for local elections. The opposition had already been barred from the elections at the time of the Caso Caja Chica investigation. November’s contests will take place amid an increase in crime, an energy crisis that is causing regular blackouts across the country, a drastic shortage of medicine in deteriorating hospitals, and regular prison massacres . “Whenever they need to get out of a crisis, they always come up with this kind of spectacle,” said Orlando Pérez, an Ecuadorian journalist and writer. Gabriela Rivadeneira, who replaced González as the Movimiento Revolución Ciudadana’s president, was also quick to react, describing González’s detention as a “kidnapping.” Meanwhile, assemblyman Xavier Lasso warned that the targets aren’t limited to Correistas but extend to doctors, students, indigenous people, businesspeople, and journalists. The Arm of a Dirty Campaign Julio César Cueva, Álvarez’s lawyer, sees a familiar pattern. “Curiously, the prosecutor’s office has this bad habit of turning cases into media spectacles first — arresting individuals, ruining them, destroying them publicly — only for those people to find out what they are being accused of after the fact,” Cueva said after González’s detention. He added that the prosecutor’s office often has “one case for the media and another for the judges.” González and Álvarez are far from the only examples of Noboa’s persecution. The biggest trophy in the president’s cabinet is Jorge Glas, Ecuador’s vice president under Correa. Glas was accused in the Caso Reconstrucción de Manabi of misusing public funds related to the emergency caused by an earthquake. He was granted asylum in Mexico but, in a scene out of a movie and in brazen violation of international law, was abducted from its embassy in Ecuador by police who invaded in the middle of the night. He is being held at Cárcel del Encuentro, a maximum security prison, and the conditions of his imprisonment have been described as systematic torture. His defense reports restricted access to hydration, significant loss of muscle mass, recurrent hunger, administration of medication by nonmedical personnel, and clear signs of malnutrition. “They’re going to bury González alive,” Correa warned . “Just as they’ve done with Aquiles Álvarez, just as they’ve done with Jorge Glas.” The recent attacks raise several questions. Is Noboa persecuting González for exposing the fruit shipments from the president’s family firm that were used for cocaine trafficking? Where is the investigation into the campaign financing inconsistencies related to Noboa’s party? Why is José Julio Neira, one of Noboa’s ministers, posting a detailed video about the Caso Laberinto? Where is the separation of powers? Where is the international community? These questions are of course largely rhetorical. Long gone are the days of Latin America’s military dictatorships, when the far right asserted control with soldiers in the streets. As Noboa is demonstrating, today’s authoritarians simply need to infiltrate a country’s democratic institutions and ensure the public prosecutor’s office answers to the executive branch. “There is a new generation of coups d’état and attacks on democratic systems,” says Alexander Madrigal, an international political scientist, professor, and researcher at the Universidad Nacional de Colombia. Forms of opposition persecution have innovated. In the era of military dictatorships, disappearances, direct actions by the state, undercover agents, etc., were a bad habit of Latin American regimes. But today we are arguably revitalizing new forms of political persecution and attacks on opposing ideas. And this is due to, or can be read as, the discrediting by the new Right. . . . . . . we’re talking about the use of the state apparatus to judicially eliminate the opposition. This is also facilitated by support from the United States. What’s Next for Ecuador? There is indeed a labyrinth in Ecuador, but it isn’t the one Noboa refers to. Rather, it is a maze of courts, mainstream media, and violence set up by the far right — one that left-wing candidates must navigate in order to achieve electoral success. By ensuring the Left can’t win at the ballot box, Noboa’s government is creating the conditions that give rise to guerrilla groups. If Ecuador is to avoid that dangerous road, the Left will have to find a way to navigate the democratic institutions increasingly co-opted by Noboa’s government. It’s a future that’s difficult to imagine without the renewal of Ecuador’s vigorous protest culture, but one not unlikely given that Noboa may have finally overplayed his hand. The road ahead is not for the faint of heart. Today’s far right in Ecuador is content to use the courts to harass and imprison left-wing leaders and bar the opposition outright. Against this backdrop, inspiration can be drawn from Assemblywoman Noriega, the member of the Movimiento Revolucion Ciudadana who double-locked her door. “We have to continue,” she said. “We have to continue with firmness, with courage. I don’t think this country needs more martyrs.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Brazil’s Working-Class President Lula Defeats Far-Right Challenger in Run-Off Election
articles.content: Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, universally known as “Lula,” defeated far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro on October 25 to win a fourth term. A former metalworker and union leader who led strikes in defiance of Brazil’s military dictatorship in the 1970s, Lula was elected to the presidency in 2002, 2006, and again in 2022 as the candidate of the Workers’ Party, a working-class party formed by the country’s unions in 1980. In a joint statement , Brazil’s main union federations declared that, “President Lula’s victory is a victory of hope and democracy. ... Throughout the country, demonstrations, marches, and gatherings multiplied. Millions of people took to the streets, of different ages, backgrounds, and experiences, united by the desire to participate in building Brazil’s future.” Bolsonaro had narrowly won the first round of the elections on October 4 with 47 percent of the vote, but with a narrow margin of victory and no candidate receiving a majority of votes, a run-off election was held three weeks later. In the run-off, Lula received 10 million more votes than in the first round, a result of the “extraordinary democratic and popular mobilization” hailed by the unions. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who attempted to instigate a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. The elder Bolsonaro was tried and convicted of plotting the coup and is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence; it was widely assumed that had his son won the presidency, he would have pardoned his father and given him a role in government. During Jair Bolsonaro’s presidency, he lowered the minimum wage, closed down the country’s Ministry of Labor, and pronounced that, “You have to do away with unions in Brazil.” He cut funding for public higher education by 30 percent and pushed through a constitutional amendment to “reform” the country’s social security system by making workers work longer and cutting retirement benefits. In contrast, Lula’s presidencies have produced material improvements in the lives of the working class which lifted millions out of poverty. In their statement, the unions point out that mobilizing for elections alone is not enough. “The force we saw in the streets needs to remain present in society and occupy space in government. We need to transform mobilization into organization, hope into participation, diversity into unity, and political energy into a permanent capacity” to propose and enact policies that can “transform” the country in interests of working people. UE has a close relationship with Brazil’s largest metalworkers’ union, CNM-CUT, which represents Wabtec workers in Brazil and has sent video greetings to several recent UE conventions.

articles.title: Socialism Matters
articles.author: Peter McLaren
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. As the midterms loom, the question of socialism becomes increasingly urgent. We are told that we live in democracies. We vote, debate, protest, and occasionally celebrate the spectacle of our collective sovereignty. Yet for most working people, democracy stops at the factory gate, the office door, the hospital corridor, and the university's administrative suite. The decisions that shape our working lives remain concentrated in the hands of owners, executives, shareholders, and managerial elites. We are invited to govern ourselves as citizens while being governed by others as workers. Here lies capitalism's great democratic contradiction: political equality is proclaimed in public while economic subordination is normalized in everyday life. Socialism matters because it asks whether democracy can remain meaningful while the economic institutions governing our lives are organized around private power. It is not simply a question of redistributing wealth after it has been accumulated, nor of asking the state to soften capitalism's cruelties. It is a question of transforming the social relations through which wealth is produced, controlled, and distributed. It asks who decides what society produces, whose needs production serves, who performs the work, and who appropriates the surplus generated by collective labor. I want to approach this question through two concepts that have become important to my own critical vocabulary: mausolocracy and ensepulcher. These terms are not decorative additions to a critique of capitalism. They are intended to perform analytical work. By mausolocracy, I mean a political-economic order in which accumulated capital and entrenched power are monumentalized, protected, and reproduced as if they were permanent features of human existence. The term evokes a mausoleum because capitalism does more than concentrate wealth: it builds institutions, laws, ideologies, and cultural arrangements that preserve the power of the living at the expense of possibilities for the living. Its monuments are not only the skyscrapers of finance, the gated enclaves of the wealthy, or the corporate empires that tower over public life. They are also the institutions that teach us to regard private ownership of productive resources as natural, economic hierarchy as inevitable, and the subordination of human needs to profitability as common sense. Mausolocracy names the architecture of this power: the institutionalized arrangements through which capital secures its authority across economic, political, cultural, and educational life. It helps explain why formal political democracy can coexist with profound economic inequality, why governments can remain responsive to concentrated wealth while claiming to represent the public, and why the accumulation of private power so often appears more politically consequential than the needs of ordinary people. Ensepulcher, by contrast, names the active process through which emancipatory alternatives are buried. If mausolocracy is the architecture of entrenched power, ensepulcher is the work required to keep that architecture standing. It operates materially, institutionally, and ideologically. It buries alternatives beneath the assertion that there is no viable alternative; it converts historically produced inequalities into apparent facts of nature; it teaches people to imagine themselves as competitors in a permanent struggle for individual survival rather than as participants in the collective transformation of society. It does not merely silence dissent. It seeks to make dissent appear futile before it begins. These concepts help us understand why socialism matters beyond the familiar arguments about taxation, public spending, or the size of government. The central issue is whether human beings can exercise democratic control over the institutions that organize their collective lives—or whether democracy will remain subordinate to the imperatives of capital. Related: Elbows Up! Canada, Trump, and the Politics of Democratic Friendship FROM WORKPLACE HIERARCHY TO WORKPLACE DEMOCRACY Richard D. Wolff offers an important point of departure. In his discussion of socialism, Wolff distinguishes regulated private capitalism, state capitalism, and forms of socialism that seek to democratize the workplace. For Wolff, an economy does not become socialist simply because the state regulates private enterprise or takes ownership of productive institutions. The deeper question concerns the relations of power within the enterprise itself. An enterprise remains capitalist when employers direct workers' labor and retain exclusive authority over the surplus that labor generates. Wolff argues that a genuinely socialist enterprise must abolish the rigid distinction between employers and employees by placing production and its proceeds under collective, democratic control. This is a crucial distinction. Socialism, in this understanding, is not merely a more generous distribution of the fruits of an otherwise unchanged economic system. It involves democratizing the process through which those fruits are produced. Workers in a democratically organized enterprise would participate in decisions about what goods and services to produce; how production should be organized; which technologies to adopt; what working conditions to establish; how necessary tasks should be shared; and how the surplus generated by their collective labor should be distributed. They would deliberate over whether that surplus should support reinvestment, improve wages and working conditions, strengthen the enterprise's long-term sustainability, or advance collectively determined social priorities. These are not minor administrative questions. They concern the allocation of human time, the organization of social cooperation, and the purposes to which productive capacity is directed. They concern whether people enter the workplace as democratic participants or as subordinates required to surrender much of their agency for the duration of the working day. Wolff's argument also challenges the assumption that state ownership alone guarantees socialism. A state-owned enterprise can reproduce hierarchical relations if officials retain authority over workers and workers remain excluded from meaningful decision-making. Public ownership can matter enormously, but ownership on paper does not automatically produce democracy in practice. The decisive question is whether people gain effective collective power over the organization of production and the distribution of its results. This does not mean that workplace democracy, by itself, resolves every problem of economic coordination, ecological sustainability, or political representation. Nor does it mean that every decision can be made without expertise, delegation, or wider social planning. It means that such arrangements must themselves be democratically accountable rather than treated as excuses for preserving the power of a minority. From the perspective of mausolocracy, the significance of workplace democracy is unmistakable: it challenges the institutional concentration of economic power. From the perspective of ensepulcher, it interrupts the burial of alternatives by demonstrating that capitalist hierarchy is not the only possible way to organize productive life. What has been constructed historically can be transformed historically. EDUCATION: REPRODUCING THE MAUSOLEUM OR OPENING ITS DOORS The struggle over socialism cannot be separated from the struggle over education. Schools and universities are not institutions floating above the economic order. They are situated within social relations that shape their funding, purposes, curricula, labor arrangements, and definitions of success. Education can help reproduce the assumptions of the existing order, but it can also become a site for questioning and transforming them. When education is increasingly subordinated to market priorities, students are encouraged to understand themselves as human capital requiring continual investment, upgrading, and competitive positioning. Knowledge is valued according to its measurable economic return. Teachers are subjected to managerial regimes of performance measurement. Universities are pressed to behave like corporations, students are recast as consumers, and the purposes of learning are narrowed to employability, productivity, and institutional prestige. The problem is not that employment, practical knowledge, or economic security are unimportant. They matter profoundly. The problem arises when these concerns become the dominant measures of education's worth, displacing its democratic, ethical, intellectual, and emancipatory purposes. Here ensepulcher becomes especially useful as an analytical concept. The educational burial of possibility occurs when students are taught—explicitly or implicitly—that social arrangements are beyond their control; that poverty is principally a personal failure; that competition is the natural condition of human existence; that the market is the ultimate arbiter of value; and that imagining a radically different society is naïve or irresponsible. The process is successful when the boundaries of what can be imagined come to resemble the boundaries of what can be done. Mausolocracy describes the larger institutional order that protects concentrated power. Ensepulcher describes the educational and ideological practices through which that order reproduces itself, including the narrowing of knowledge, the marginalization of dissent, and the conversion of historically contingent social arrangements into seemingly permanent truths. Yet education is never simply a machine for reproducing domination. Its contradictions can open spaces for critical inquiry, collective reflection, and democratic struggle. Teachers and students can examine how economic power shapes the conditions of learning, whose knowledge is legitimized, whose histories are excluded, and what forms of human possibility are rendered invisible. FREIRE, REVOLUTIONARY CRITICAL PEDAGOGY, AND THE STRUGGLE AGAINST ENSEPULCHER Paulo Freire's critique of the banking model of education remains indispensable here. In Pedagogy of the Oppressed, Freire challenges an educational relationship in which teachers deposit knowledge into passive students, treating learners as receptacles rather than as subjects capable of interpreting and transforming their world. Against this model, he advances dialogical, problem-posing education grounded in critical reflection and action. Freire's contribution is not simply a more humane teaching technique. It is a challenge to relations of domination embedded in the production of knowledge. Students must be able to investigate the social conditions shaping their lives, recognize contradictions, and develop the capacity to act collectively upon them. Learning becomes inseparable from praxis: the dialectical relationship between reflection and action. But a critical pedagogy adequate to the present must also ask how educational institutions are situated within the wider organization of capitalist society. It must investigate ownership, class relations, the appropriation of surplus, and the ways capitalism intersects with racism, patriarchy, colonialism, and other structures of domination. It must examine not only what is taught but also who controls the institution, whose labor sustains it, which communities benefit from it, and whose needs remain subordinated. This is where my work on revolutionary critical pedagogy enters the argument. In my dialogue with Glenn Rikowski, Pedagogy for Revolution against Education for Capital , we addressed the relationship between education and the capitalist social relations within which it operates. That relationship cannot be adequately understood by treating educational inequality as a collection of isolated problems to be corrected while leaving the underlying organization of economic power untouched. A revolutionary critical pedagogy does not simply ask how education can help individuals succeed within the existing order. It asks how education can contribute to collective struggles capable of transforming the conditions that produce inequality in the first place. It seeks to make visible the social relations hidden behind apparently neutral arrangements, while developing the intellectual and political capacities necessary for collective agency. In this sense, revolutionary critical pedagogy contests ensepulcher directly. It brings buried possibilities back into public consciousness. It asks students to consider why workplaces are organized hierarchically, why some people command the labor of others, why productive abundance coexists with deprivation, and why decisions affecting millions are often made without meaningful democratic participation by those most affected. It does not promise that critical awareness automatically produces social transformation. Nor does it reduce education to political indoctrination. Its purpose is to make rigorous inquiry, historical understanding, ethical deliberation, and collective action possible—so that existing arrangements can be examined rather than simply accepted. A socialist educational vision would therefore require more than changing classroom content. It would also require confronting the material conditions of education: unequal access to resources, the exploitation and precarity of educational labor, the privatization of public goods, and the growing influence of corporate interests over institutional priorities. Emancipatory teaching cannot substitute for the transformation of unjust material conditions. But without critical education, those conditions are more likely to be reproduced as unquestioned common sense. FROM REVOLUTIONARY TO PROPHETIC CRITICAL PEDAGOGY My subsequent work with Petar Jandrić on revolutionary critical pedagogy and liberation theology extends this argument into an explicitly ethical and spiritual register. In From Liberation to Salvation: Revolutionary Critical Pedagogy Meets Liberation Theology , we explored the relationship between Marxist critique, liberation theology, solidarity with the oppressed, and the possibility of a transformed social order. Liberation theology insists that the suffering of the poor cannot be treated as an incidental cost of social progress or as a matter of private charity alone. It demands that the structures producing suffering be confronted. Its ethical challenge is inseparable from a material critique of the institutions that organize wealth, power, and exclusion. In this respect, it enters into a profound conversation with revolutionary critical pedagogy: both insist that the denunciation of injustice must be joined to practices that make liberation possible. This connection informs what I call prophetic critical pedagogy. The prophetic is not a prediction that history will automatically deliver a just society. It is a refusal to accept the present as the final horizon of human possibility. It joins the denunciation of oppressive realities to the annunciation of a more humane future, while recognizing that such a future must be created through struggle, solidarity, ethical commitment, and collective action. The distinction matters. Revolutionary critical pedagogy investigates and challenges the material and ideological relations that reproduce domination. Prophetic critical pedagogy carries that critique into a horizon of moral responsibility: it asks what kind of world we are obligated to struggle toward, whose suffering demands our attention, and what forms of solidarity are required if human dignity is to mean more than an abstract declaration. Liberation theology deepens this challenge by placing the lives of the poor and oppressed at the center of moral and political judgment. It contests the idolatry of money and the treatment of accumulation as an unquestionable social good. It insists that economic arrangements must be judged by their consequences for human beings, especially those whose labor and suffering are routinely rendered invisible. This is why the question of socialism cannot be confined to economic efficiency or institutional design. It is also a question of the kind of society we are willing to build, the forms of suffering we are willing to tolerate, and the responsibilities we recognize toward one another. A society may possess extraordinary productive capacity and still fail morally if that capacity is organized to preserve privilege while leaving people without the conditions necessary to live with dignity. SOCIALISM AS THE DEMOCRATIZATION OF POSSIBILITY Socialism must, of course, be approached critically rather than idealized. Its name alone does not guarantee democracy, justice, or freedom. Historical projects claiming socialist legitimacy have sometimes concentrated authority in the state, suppressed dissent, or preserved hierarchical workplace relations. These failures must be confronted honestly. Socialism worthy of the name must be judged by the actual democratic power it enables people to exercise, the freedoms it protects, and its capacity to meet human needs without reproducing new forms of domination. Wolff's emphasis on workplace democracy offers one important criterion: people should not be excluded from decisions that govern their working lives and determine what happens to the value they collectively create. Freire offers another: education should cultivate the capacity to read the world critically rather than merely adapt to it. Revolutionary critical pedagogy asks how these capacities can contribute to transforming the social relations that reproduce exploitation. Prophetic critical pedagogy asks what ethical commitments should guide that transformation and whose liberation must remain at its center. Together, these approaches help clarify the analytical relationship between mausolocracy and ensepulcher. Mausolocracy names the architecture of entrenched power; ensepulcher names the active burial of alternatives that helps sustain it. Revolutionary critical pedagogy investigates and contests the material and ideological mechanisms of that reproduction. Prophetic critical pedagogy connects such critique to a moral horizon of solidarity, liberation, and human possibility. The task, then, is not simply to make capitalism more tolerable while leaving its central relations of power intact. It is to democratize the institutions through which social life is organized, to expand the capacity of people to shape the conditions of their existence, and to reclaim education as a practice through which we learn to understand and transform the world we share. Socialism matters because democracy should not end where economic power begins. It matters because the people who collectively produce society's wealth should have a meaningful voice in determining how that wealth is used. It matters because education should do more than prepare people to occupy predetermined positions within an unequal order: it should help them understand why that order exists and how it might be changed. The mausoleum of capital is not invulnerable. Its apparent permanence depends upon institutions, practices, and beliefs that are historically made and therefore open to historical struggle. Ensepulcher is never complete, because the possibilities it seeks to bury can be recovered through critical thought, collective action, and solidarity. The purpose of revolutionary and prophetic critical pedagogy is not to decorate that mausoleum with the language of justice. It is to help dismantle the conditions that make it possible—and to participate in building a world in which the freedom and flourishing of each become inseparable from the freedom and flourishing of all.
