articles.title: Nuclear war and climate change
articles.author: Tom Engelhardt
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I’ve read the New York Times since I was a teenager. It was once a way to keep up on the news. It’s now a daily way to experience a living nightmare of a world. I’m thinking, of course, of Donald Trump’s world—although it could be Vladimir Putin’s, too—and that’s just to start down an ever-lengthening grim list. This, in all honesty, is not the world that anyone should want to be on at a time when humanity has discovered at least two ways of doing this planet in, the slow-motion version known as climate change and the (more or less) instantaneous version of nuclear war. And in this strange world of ours, who honestly knows what Artificial Intelligence, or AI, might be able to do when it comes to creating a potential third pathway to ultimate destruction? (Not this old man, that’s for sure.) Consider it strange, given that nuclear weapons are clearly also doomsday ones, that, in the 80-plus years since the U.S. dropped two of them on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki with devastating effect, including the deaths of more than 200,000 people (almost 40,000 of them believed to have been children), nine countries have come to possess far more devastating versions of just such weaponry. It’s now estimated that there are more than 12,000 nuclear weapons on this planet, with the U.S. and Russia each believed to possess more than 5,000. That’s enough, of course, to destroy any number of planets, with most of those weapons six to 50 times more powerful than the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima. Worse yet, their cumulative numbers only continue to grow in this world of ours, and they are ever more devastatingly powerful. Given our history over all these centuries (and the global hellscapes we’ve already created), what could possibly go wrong? Count on this (if you’re still counting): in the near future, the number of countries in possession of such weaponry will undoubtedly only rise again . Once upon a time, end-of-the-world scenarios were nightmarish fantasies of fiction, the sort of thing that novelists like George Orwell or Aldous Huxley came up with and that I read with fascination in my youth. Buy the Book Now, who needs a dystopian novel when, just sitting down each morning (or evening) to read the Times , as I still do (one day late, of course, since I read the paper version, which says plenty about this old man), has a strangely end-of-world feeling to it? After all, we humans have come up with at least a second (slow-motion) way to do in ourselves and every other living thing on this planet that has gained the all too mild label “climate change.” Why it’s not “climate devastation,” “climate destruction,” “climate catastrophe,” or something even worse? Change, really? Gee, climate mutation doesn’t sound so bad either, does it? In mid-October, as I was starting this piece, I went out on my daily early morning walk in New York City, wearing just khakis, a long-sleeved shirt, and a light jacket. By 8:30, I had already tied my jacket around my waist and rolled up my shirt sleeves—and I still felt slightly uncomfortable. I know, I know, any passingly hot day or even a warm few weeks doesn’t truly prove a thing. Still, only recently, record highs were “forecast to stretch all across the central and eastern United States, with temperatures running about 20 degrees above average, according to Weather.com meteorologist Rob Shackelford.” In addition, the British medical magazine The Lancet ‘s Commission on 21st Century Global Threats recently offered this apocalyptic scenario ( as reported by The Guardian ): “’Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,’ the report said, adding that, while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons.” And as Jeet Heer recently pointed out at The Nation magazine, “AI is clearly the most dangerous technology that humankind has developed since nuclear weapons, and our current lack of oversight for it is a travesty.” Am I surprised? Not really...sigh... Related: Trump's Imperial Decline: America in Retreat Living in a Dystopian Novel of a World In truth, I’m already too damn old to genuinely grasp that third possibility for ultimate destruction, involving AI— though anything AI-related makes me instantaneously anxious as hell. Though it’s not possible anymore to avoid AI if you’re simply looking for something online, I still do my damnedest (so to speak) to avoid it otherwise, since I prefer to be on a planet where the best and worst things in life aren’t caused by some almost unimaginable computer-created irreality—or do I mean surreality, since this world seems (thank you Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin!) ever more surreal in all too many ways? Of course, here’s the truly strange thing: Can you explain to me what kind of creatures would plan for, pour funding into, and work to create anything-but-obvious or easy-to-produce ways of bringing about their own extermination, not to speak of that of all life around them? I know, I know, that first way of doing us all in, atomic weaponry, still passes for war . But explain to me, what a country could possibly win with more than 5,000 nuclear weapons. Honestly, how mad can you be to purposely create ever more world-ending weaponry to—yes!—(theoretically) defend yourself? And then, of course, we humans put in power characters like Donald Trump, who, at the U.N. this September, implicitly threatened to use such weaponry to “annihilate” Iran, or Vladimir Putin, who has actually threatened to use nuclear weapons in any future conflict with other European powers that might develop out of his war on Ukraine. Ask yourself, would you really choose to put either of their trigger fingers on the American or Russian nuclear arsenals? And how much madder do you have to be, as president of the United States (no less), than to put so much of your extra energy into promoting anything that will burn down (or do I mean burn up) this planet of ours? That, of course, is what “our” president is now doing when it comes to the full-scale promotion of the ever greater use of oil, coal, and natural gas. And, of course, he not only continues to essentially deny that climate change is even happening, but at the U.N. last year called it “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world.” Consider him nothing short of a promoter (of course, who doesn’t know that he’s a promoter?) of a world-ending reality—or do I mean surreality? Related: Trump's America: Failing, Flailing, and Falling Honestly, I’d like to bring George Orwell and Aldous Huxley back from the dead so many years later, because I’d love to read Orwell’s next novel: 2030 or Huxley’s Brave New Trump ( or, for that matter, Brave New Putin ). And give me some credit here, since I haven’t even bothered you with the possibility that India and Pakistan, both nuclear-armed, could someday engage in a globally devastating “limited” nuclear war, creating what’s known as a “nuclear winter” on this planet that might kill not just Indians and Pakistanis but billions of the rest of us. In truth, if this heavily nuclear-armed world of ours and leaders like Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin weren’t our reality, this piece would be the most unbelievable kind of dystopian fiction around. And yet, keep in mind that, at this very moment, given climate change, we’re already experiencing a slow-motion version of nuclear-style disaster on this planet of ours. Hopefully, I’m (mis)reading the times (as well as The Times ) when it comes to our future nuclear peril. Unfortunately, when it comes to the slow-motion version of nuclear war, which we call climate change and the overheating of this planet of ours, a distinctly dystopian future is already well underway. Tom's Substack

articles.title: Chicago wrongful convictions
articles.author: Michael Steven Smith
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In October 2026, the Chicago City Council authorized payment via plaintiff Anand. Swaminathan’s law firm Loevy and Loevy of $260.8 million That is over a quarter of $1 billion dollars in compensation for the wrongful murder convictions of the firm’s clients, 17 young men years ago. This settlement against the Chicago Police Department is the largest in the city’s history. They collectively served nearly 400 years in prison for murders for which they were falsely convicted. Attorney Swaminathan and his partner Steve Art litigated their cases for 13 years. The false convictions of murder were arranged by Chicago police detective Reynaldo Guevarra. He was responsible for some 50 convictions, all the frame-ups were accomplishedby using false witness statements, and false coerced confessions. The victims lived in the heavily Latino community of Chicago’s Northwest side in the 1980s and 1990s. The victims are all young men ages 14 to 28. Related: Malcolm X at 100: The Movement for Black Lives Detective Guevara is retired. He lives on a Police Department pension of $91,000 a year and will likely never be held accountable. The passage of time and the unavailability and death of witnesses has so far, got him off the hook. When he was deposed he took the Fifth Amendment some 200 times. Before detective Ronaldo Guevara was sending innocent Latino men to prison, his counterpart Chicago Police Department Commander John Burge was torturing Black men on the southwest side to confess falsely to an array of crimes. This was exposed in litigation and community activism by civil rights attorney Flint Taylor and his law firm the Peoples Law Office. He wrote about it in his book, “The Torture Machine“. With solitary organizing and support, Taylor was able to get a prison sentence for Burge based on perjury. Comedian Lenny Bruce used to say “Chicago is so corrupt it’s thrilling.” Is it possible to reform the police ? What part does racism play? How much money have the citizens of Chicago been forced to pay by the actions of the police department? Will this gargantuan settlement actually bring about reforms? Do the powers that be in Chicago really want reforms? Related: Trump’s Versailles on the Potomac The most fundamental reform would be community control of the police instead of allowing them to terrorize the Black community. Anand Swaminathan grew up in Madison, Wisconsin, the son of immigrant Indian parents who were professors. He attended Harvard law school, where he had more cases in its legal aid efforts than any previous student at the school. Swaminathan is a partner at a law firm of Loevy and Loevy, where he has worked for the last 16 years. Before Swaminathan could sue on behalf of his clients he had to get them he exonerated and released from prison. This was accomplished through the work of Exhonoration Project sponsored by his law firm working with Northwestern University Law School. Overall, this victory and the prior one on police torture would not have happened without the informed and active community in Chicago.

articles.title: Fatherland Feels Both Ancient and Tragically Contemporary
articles.author: Corey Robin
articles.content: Fatherland , the new Paweł Pawlikowski film about Thomas Mann’s 1949 trip to Germany, may be the most powerful film about the current moment — really, the last ten years — that I’ve seen. It’s not about the current moment at all, in fact. It’s about Mann’s olympian, and doomed, effort to remain a man of culture, a voice of liberal civilization in the face of that civilization’s total collapse. In other words, it’s about the current moment. As Thomas and his daughter, Erika Mann, played by the brilliant Sandra Hüller, tour a Germany divided in two and still struggling to get back on its feet, they confront the detritus of the barbarism that has consumed Europe and the gentility of the collaborators who helped bring that barbarism about. The relationship of the Manns to those collaborators is personal: one is an ex-husband of Erika, another two (the grandchildren of Richard Wagner) look to Thomas as their patron saint and potential savior. Played by the also brilliant Hanns Zischler, Thomas Mann slices through the screen with a stiletto of irony, honed across decades of urbane detachment and sly observation. His honorable refusal to collaborate with the Nazis gives him a passport to cross borders while remaining aloof and above the evil that guards the gates. He is devastatingly cool toward his enemies without suffering their discomfort or disturbance. He’s also repeatedly exposed, most powerfully by his daughter and by a lonely dissenter in the eastern zone of the country, as a preening moralist. The futility of his refusal, the fecklessness of his resistance, are as pronounced as the serenity of his self-regard. Never has the liberal humanist seemed so entitled to our respect — and so incapable of holding it. Amid the moral catastrophe of the film, it’s tempting to look to Erika as its moral center. She confronts her father in a scene that is as devastating as any of his confrontations with the Nazis. Yet she, in her way, is as attached to the myth of Thomas Mann as he is. She stays with him throughout his trip, while her beloved brother, Klaus, who has begged her to come to his protection, spirals downward into suicide. We’re left uncertain, by the film’s end, whether she and her father will attend Klaus’s funeral. Her voice and actions are as compromised as her father’s, and as ours. With its stripped-down aesthetics, its swift story telling and immediate shades of black and white, Fatherland tells the story of an entire era in roughly an hour of film. It achieves an almost mythical stature, summoning an inheritance that extends from the ancient Greeks to the Germans. The fate of Mann, the father, recalls Wagner’s Götterdämmerung , the twilight of the gods who are no longer fit or able to rule the world and thus lose their place in it. In the film, Mann carries a tradition that has proven completely incapable of fending off the most terrible evils. While many have returned in recent years to the literature and biography of Mann — most notably Colm Tóibín in his wonderful novel The Magician (Tóibín is thanked in the film’s credits) — no one, aside from Pawlikowski, has looked to Mann as, or made him into, such a disturbing exemplar of the feebleness of liberalism in our current moment. The relationship between Thomas and Erika also recalls Wagner’s Die Walküre , where the love of an olympian father, Wotan, for his beloved daughter, Brünnhilde — like Erika, Brünnhilde seeks to protect her half-brother, Siegmund, but fails in doing so — is ultimately destroyed by her disobedience of Wotan. In Fatherland , it is Klaus’s suicide that rips open a painful tear in the fabric between of Erika and Thomas. Reaching further back, Fatherland recalls Sophocles’s Oedipus cycle, particularly the second and third plays in the trilogy. In Antigone , Oedipus’s daughter Antigone struggles to honor her brother, Polynices, who has been killed in battle and is denied a proper funeral by the new king, Creon. Erika’s fidelity to and love for her brother, her anguish over his suicide, and the question of whether she and Thomas will attend his funeral — all of this recalls the struggle of Antigone. Oedipus at Colonus , the third play, in which Antigone accompanies her father Oedipus, now exiled, also figures in Fatherland . Oedipus, of course, is now blind, as is Thomas Mann, in his way. Despite these ancient and mythic resonances, it is the contemporaneity of the film that presses itself upon us. Both Erika and Thomas Mann struggle to maintain their composure and their integrity, but each betrays their values, suggesting how difficult it is to remain a moral being in an immoral world. The father toggles between nobility and narcissism, the daughter between judgment and despair. The last scene conveys the terrible futility and sadness of it all, the music of Bach painfully sounding as a register of the desolation enveloping us. articles.title: France’s Rulers Want Violence as a Pretext for a Crackdown
articles.author: Marlon Ettinger
articles.content: The French government was almost desperate for something to happen. Over the weekend, the social movement that started with a series of high school blockades in mid-September continued with a well-attended, orderly march around the outskirts of Paris. The protest route, initially scheduled and approved to take place between the central Place de la Bastille and Place de la Nation, was shifted to a path between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes, a route along the southeastern rim of the city that traces the highway that encircles Paris. The modified route for October 24 took around 110,000 marchers away from the center of Paris, where, the previous weekend, impressive scenes of mobilization at symbolic locales like Bastille and Les Invalides had demonstrated the expansion of the social movement. At least half a million people had already marched on October 17 across France, brandishing slogans demonstrating against the high cost of living, the fuel price crisis, and the rise of the far right, as well as in support of the demands of France’s high schoolers. In the evening of October 17, violent confrontations between the police and some protesters had accelerated, and the police appeared to lose control of the streets. Hundreds of businesses were looted and burned in Paris by a combination of black bloc and autonomist militants as well as opportunistic vandals. In the lead-up to this Saturday’s march, a steady drumbeat of condemnation came from the world’s governments and ruling class. A wave of racist bile swept from the White House across the governments of Europe, grotesquely laying the blame for every instance of looting or vandalism on France’s Arab and African population. Ignored, or condescended to, were millions of people’s demands to improve conditions in high schools; to avoid another budget with over €50 billion worth of cuts and the steady chipping away of the country’s social system; or to address the multiplication of crises facing the country. Instead the government fretted nervously about the potential for more violence on October 24, establishing days-long curfews from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. across multiple big cities and mobilizing ten thousand additional police officers. Sébastien Lecornu, the prime minister, even met with the directors of some of France’s largest telecoms firms to prepare them to cut off access to social media like TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, and Twitter. “If I give the instruction, proceed without delay to temporarily suspend the concerned services for a duration of a few hours,” Lecornu wrote to the companies. The government’s anticipation that October 24 would inevitably degrade into the same chaos of the week before echoed its line since the student movement began. France’s leadership believes that so-called far left forces like France Insoumise are orchestrating the aboveground movement to create conditions of chaos that their proxies in the “ultraleft,” which include a variety of autonomist and anarchist movements like black bloc, can exploit to topple the government. “There was a plan in place organized by small, far-left groupings, encouraged from the National Assembly by France Insoumise. . . . to destabilize the Republic, to bring down the government, . . . [the] state that protects honest people, which allows you to go shop for groceries on Saturday,” fulminated Laurent Marcangeli ahead of Saturday’s march. Marcangeli, an MP from Corsica, is the president of the centrist party Horizons, founded as a vehicle for Édouard Philippe, President Emmanuel Macron’s first prime minister and currently the leading (though sinking) contender to represent the right and center in next year’s presidential election. France Insoumise, Marcangeli claimed, is nothing more than the legal branch of this “galaxy” of ultraleft organizations, and its leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has an insurrectionary attitude that could lead the country toward civil war. Marcangeli also called for France Insoumise to fund the repairs for the damage caused by the rioting. Claiming that the party stands by the rioters, he pointed to the €4 million that France Insoumise’s elected officials receive in public money, saying that it came from “our taxes.” Potential Energy As it turned out, October 24 stayed largely calm, though there were some confrontations between police and protesters at Paris’s Place de la Nation, which the police kept cordoned off tightly. Around 6 p.m. I was in the area and tried to see what was going on down a street filled with tear gas and booms , but was pushed away gently but firmly by four shouting police officers. After stepping into a café just around the corner, I saw dramatic images of protesters facing off against police officers and tear gas on the television. They were showing the street I had been on just a minute before, but their video feed made the street look like there was a lot less light than I could clearly see from my view outside the café window. Earlier in the day in the crowd by Porte de Vincennes, Philippe, a sixty-six-year-old Parisian, told me that the images being commented on around the world were basically just “goddamn propaganda.” ”It’s politicians who benefit from this,” Philippe said, “in particular far-right politicians who can say voilà , France is going badly because of immigrants. But it’s not immigrants, it’s French people [who are protesting].” The propaganda is spread by social media and the TV, he says, because people who “want power” want it. “It’s bulls–t, it’s television, it’s the media who show all these images of brawling in the streets, but meanwhile very few people actually participate [in it,]” Philippe said. “I protested [last week] and I didn’t see a single [riot cop] where I was.” Throughout the day, mainstream media fed the flames with speculation about what might happen after the sun went down. They stuck to this story even as masses of people flowed peacefully across bridges and over the tram tracks along the route, unmoved by the steady rainfall or the constant muted drone of low-flying helicopters hovering watchfully in the skies above. CNEWS, the reactionary cable news network owned by the pro–Marine Le Pen billionaire Vincent Bolloré, even broadcast a video of protesters pulling on masks next to footage of sturdy rows of riot police, predicting that this signaled an imminent outbreak of violence. “These protesters are changing their clothes,” CNEWS journalist Olivier Benkemoun commented as the camera ranged over a scene of upbeat demonstrators. “That’s significant. You’re in a protest march and suddenly you have people acting like future vandals, like future rioters.” “They’re equipping themselves,” he added breathlessly, sounding shocked. ”You’re seeing it live — helmets, balaclavas, masks. . . . it’s happening right beneath the eyes of the camera.” Within twenty minutes, Benkemoun offered a correction live on air. The footage wasn’t from Paris, but from Tirana in Albania, easily identified by a distinctive mural near the country’s Ministry of Education, Sport, and Youth. “That wasn’t Paris,” Benkemoun said. “I’d like to apologize on behalf of the editorial staff because the images of those people wearing masks came from Albania.” Did it matter though? “That doesn’t change anything,” the presenter chimed in response. “It’s the same technique,” Benkemoun agreed. Presidential Elections When I asked Philippe why he thinks this social movement in particular appears to be significant, he said it was because we’re in the lead-up to an election year. Next spring’s presidential election is never far from the surface in any discussion about the protests. After the October 17 march and rioting, Marine Le Pen and her party, Rassemblement National, leaped gleefully at the opportunity to present themselves as the party of order. Le Pen quickly filmed a stern, authoritative speech from behind a large, serious desk where she talked about the measures a Rassemblement National government would take against rioters. “We embody a peaceful France and an orderly France in the face of left-wing extremists,” Rassemblement National deputy Julien Odoul said at the party congress in Orléans, which also began on Saturday. In the meantime, the French government went into overdrive attacking France Insoumise for its alleged role in the violence. Despite its clear support for the high schoolers’ protest movement from the beginning, it’s unclear how exactly France Insoumise was connected to the violence. The government’s narrative rests on leaked intelligence reports from early on in the movement, claiming that the high schoolers were being coordinated by France Insoumise and their “proxies” in the “ultraleft.” Intelligence officers involved in those assessments later told investigative outlet Mediapart that they felt pressured by higher-ups to produce evidence of the link. Ahead of the October 24 march, Macron announced that requests to protest “by people without any legitimacy would be banned.” It was a clear message that the “ultraleft” groups who the government has blamed for the violence would be cracked down on with extreme force. But it’s also part of an escalating crackdown against France Insoumise, who are being linked more and more explicitly with the so-called ultraleft, despite clear strategic differences and even goals between this nebulous designation and France Inoumise. “Its importance is overestimated,” the political scientist Arthur Pouliquen told Le Monde in an analysis published over the weekend. “Those who share our struggle have no business being involved in looting and ransacking,” Mélenchon said after October 17, insisting on the movement’s nonviolent character. “We must refuse to participate in actions which have no political significance and which are contrary to our methods.” Nevertheless, the Le Monde analysis highlighted some links, calling France Insoumise the “umbrella” for both the “far left” and the “ultraleft.” Le Monde clarified that the party is neither of these things, but that they enjoy “harmonious” relations with the far-left camp, in the words of Frustration Magazine editor-in-chief Nicolas Framont. ”In an extremely polarized political landscape, [France Insoumise] plays the role of an “umbrella” party for this political camp, often acting as the de facto representative of the antiestablishment,” Le Monde concludes. The idea that France Insoumise is merely the legal arm of an insurrectionary, prerevolutionary or now close-to-revolutionary left has gained currency on the center and the right in the week since the violence on October 17. More than one powerful member of the government has raised the idea of banning them all together. The latest to raise the question was the president of France’s Senate, Gérard Larcher , who’s second in line to the presidency. “Beware to those who seek insurrection,” Larcher told Le Figaro on October 19. France Insoumise “has been stoking the flames. . . . they bear a large part of the responsibility for this hateful discourse, the question of [banning them] can be posed.” This article originally appeared in Jacobin , a democratic socialist magazine publishing long-form essays and analysis on politics, economics, and culture. articles.title: Airbnb LA elections
articles.author: Robin Urevich
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. The Airbnb-sponsored Committee to Expand the Middle Class is one of the biggest spenders in local elections this year, contributing about 30 times more than it has in all previous Los Angeles elections combined since 2018. The short-term rental giant has upped its political spending across the country since last year, pouring $7.1 million so far into this year’s L.A. mayor’s race and three other local contests as of mid-October. Airbnb’s contributions to local independent expenditure committees support Mayor Karen Bass’ reelection campaign and those of three other local candidates: John McKinney for city attorney and City Council candidates Tim Gaspar in District 3 in the west San Fernando Valley and Jose Ugarte in District 9 in South Los Angeles. The company also backed incumbent Traci Park in City Council District 11 on L.A.’s Westside, who won outright in the June primary. The outpouring of cash comes as the company has lobbied the city to permit additional short-term rentals for a limited time ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games. Bass favors the expansion. Her challenger, L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, didn’t respond to Capital & Main emails inquiring about her stance on the issue. But in an October candidate forum , she criticized Bass’ support for loosening short-term rental restrictions. Raman has led City Council efforts to strengthen enforcement of L.A.’s current law. Airbnb spokesperson Justin Wesson said in a statement that the unprecedented spending in L.A. politics this year is part of Airbnb’s nationwide effort to “back causes and candidates that champion building local economies, including a tourism economy that doesn’t just benefit big, corporate hotels, but also everyday homeowners looking to make extra money by sharing their home.” As of mid-October, Airbnb’s election spending rivals that of hedge fund manager Aaron Sosnick, an advocate of adding bike lanes to L.A. streets, who had donated about $7 million to committees backing Raman as of early October. Airbnb has so far overtaken the Los Angeles Police Protective League — traditionally one of the largest contributors to local elections — in political giving. The Police Protective League had spent more than $4 million on committees supporting Bass, McKinney, Gaspar, Ugarte and others as of early October. “They [Airbnb] are trying to buy the election,” said Estuardo Mazariegos, a City Council candidate for South Los Angeles who opposes an increase in short-term rentals in the city. Airbnb donated $750,000 to a political action committee sponsored by the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 18, which supports Ugarte, Mazariegos’ opponent. Independent expenditure committees, unlike individual donors, can spend unlimited amounts in elections — as long as they don’t coordinate their activities with candidates’ campaigns. The Airbnb committee gave more than $6.1 million to political action committees sponsored by the Central City Association, a downtown L.A.-based nonprofit that promotes business interests. A $750,000 contribution went to a Central City Association committee that backs Bass, while $3.3 million was earmarked for CCA-sponsored committees that support city attorney candidate McKinney. Related: The St. George Hotel Shows How Los Angeles Can Lose Affordable Housing While Fighting Homelessness Airbnb’s political largesse has so far yielded a win for the company in California’s Orange County in June and mixed results in Dallas and New York City last year. But Airbnb may be seeking a more dominant role in Los Angeles politics, given the magnitude of its campaign contributions. In Dallas, the company poured $500,000 into its Revitalize Dallas PAC to back three City Council candidates last year. Only one candidate won. After New York City passed a 2023 law strictly limiting short-term rentals, Airbnb’s Affordable New York PAC spent nearly $4 million backing 17 winning candidates in local races and opposing Zohran Mamdani’s successful mayoral bid. The company’s spending on statewide California issues and candidates is also way up, from $2.2 million in 2024 to almost $7.7 million as of Oct. 22. Airbnb’s Citizens for an Affordable California independent expenditure committee spent more than $1.3 million in a successful effort to force Orange County Democratic state Assembly candidate Mark Pulido into a runoff next month against Republican candidate Paolo Morales. Related: How Santa Monica Makes Section 8 Housing Work In L.A., Airbnb’s political spending appears to be part of a broader push to shape local policy. Over 18 months, the company has spent almost $4.2 million lobbying, primarily for a proposed vacation rental ordinance. The Vacation Rental Ordinance could temporarily expand L.A.’s short-term rental market by as many as 15,000 units ahead of the 2028 Olympic Games. The law would sunset in December 2028, five months after the games’ scheduled closing ceremony. The city’s current home sharing law permits Angelenos to offer only their primary residences for rent to nightly or weekly visitors. The proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance would temporarily override that provision and permit residents to rent second homes to tourists. In a January letter to the L.A. City Council, Wesson argued that passing such an ordinance could bring the city a windfall of up to $110 million in additional transient occupancy or bed taxes on nightly tourist stays. As part of its lobbying effort, Airbnb brought together labor unions, local chambers of commerce and community groups in support of the proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance. Airbnb called the coalition “Save Our Services” and spent almost $3.7 million of its lobbying dollars for its “media” and “canvassing” expenses, according to L.A. City Ethics Commission disclosures. More than a dozen members of the Airbnb coalition — from the organizers of a Koreatown cultural festival to the Crenshaw Chamber of Commerce — echoed Wesson’s argument at a May 12 meeting of the City Council’s Planning and Land Use Committee. Kevin Norton of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 18 asked, “Does it make sense for our city to keep saying we have no money for critical needs while blocking a proven source of income?” Norton added that the city could collect “up to $110 million dollars [in tax revenue] that are projected” and urged lawmakers to “be fiscally smart” and “amend the short term rental ordinance.” Related: Toxic Smoke, Corporate Power and Neglect in Boyle Heights But the proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance — which has been under discussion at the City Council since 2018 — wouldn’t generate additional revenue, said Vincent Bertoni, L.A. director of city planning, in a 2021 memo to the City Council. The proposed law would do nothing to attract more visitors to the city, Bertoni said; instead, it would simply give travelers more places to stay. In April, Bertoni said in another memo that the supply of second homes isn’t large enough to significantly increase tax revenues. In his letter to the City Council, Wesson argued that additional vacation rentals would help the city accommodate Olympics spectators at a time when hotels would be stretched to capacity. That’s one reason Bass said she supports the measure. Neither Bass nor her challenger, Raman, responded to Capital & Main’s interview requests or questions about their positions on the proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance. But in May, Bass told NBC4 that the policy would “accommodate the influx of tourists during the Olympics.” Bass emphasized the short-term rental expansion would be temporary. “Otherwise I would be concerned about the housing supply,” she said. For her part, at an Oct. 3 Caló News-sponsored candidate forum in South L.A., Raman said she will “make sure this mayor’s push for deregulating short-term rentals during this time in ways that are harmful to renters don’t go through.” At the May Planning and Land Use Committee meeting, three hotel managers said there was no need to expand short-term rentals because their hotels had ample rooms to accommodate visitors to the Olympic Games. A September report commissioned by the Hotel Association of Los Angeles said “6 in 10 hoteliers expect short-term rental … growth to hurt bookings & rates.” Related: Who Polices the ICE Detention Centers? In McFarland, GEO Group Appears to Police Itself In 2018, L.A. adopted its Home Sharing Ordinance, which allows Angelenos to offer only their primary residences for nightly or weekly rentals. That same year, then-City Councilmember Herb Wesson — Justin Wesson’s father — and current City Council President Marqueece Harris-Dawson first proposed adding second homes to the short-term rental market. City Councilmember Bob Blumenfield, who chairs the City Council’s Planning and Land Use Committee, told Capital & Main he opposed the idea of allowing second homes to be used as short-term rentals eight years ago and still does today. He said the proposal could incentivize some landlords to turn housing into tourist accommodations. “The actual cost to the city when you lose affordable housing can be much greater than any benefit we might see in taxes for opening up vacation rentals,” Blumenfield said. The current vacation rental proposal has safeguards to prevent people from purchasing second homes to use as short-term rentals. But Blumenfield said the law would be difficult to enforce. The city lacks sufficient staff to enforce its current home sharing law, according to a 2024 L.A. Housing Department report, which estimated that 7,500 short-term rentals in multifamily buildings operated illegally. That same year, a Capital & Main and ProPublica investigation found dozens of rent-controlled apartments — which cannot legally be offered for nightly or weekly rentals — were nonetheless available on vacation rental booking sites such as booking.com . Several were also listed on Airbnb, despite an agreement the company has with the city to share listings data and remove illegal listings from its platform. At the time, an Airbnb spokesperson said, “there is no place on Airbnb for Hosts who circumvent the City’s Home-Sharing Ordinance and we will continue to work closely with city staff to address Hosts who try to evade the rules.” Blumenfield said he won’t hold a hearing on the vacation rental proposal until city departments report to the City Council with plans for strengthening enforcement of the current home sharing law. The City Council’s Housing and Homelessness Committee requested those reports nearly two years ago, but city departments have yet to provide them in full. Blumenfield’s chairmanship of the committee will end in December, when he reaches the council’s three-term limit. The fate of the vacation rental proposal may depend on which candidates for mayor and City Council are elected on November 3. Airbnb-backed City Council candidates Ugarte and Gaspar didn’t respond to Capital & Main’s questions about their positions on the proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance. McKinney, the candidate Airbnb supports for city attorney, also didn’t respond to questions about how he would approach home sharing enforcement. Westside resident Ellen Evans, who supports stronger short-term rental enforcement, chairs the Bel Air-Beverly Crest Neighborhood Council, one of three local elected neighborhood councils that have registered their opposition to the proposed Vacation Rental Ordinance at the City Council. Evans said she was speaking to Capital & Main as a private citizen, not as a representative of her neighborhood council. “It’s really hard for the council members to justify this [the Vacation Rental Ordinance] in a city with a huge housing crisis,” Evans said. “I feel reasonably confident they’ll make the right choice.” Capital & Main

articles.title: Crackdown on Pro-Palestinian Speech
articles.author: Stephen Rohde
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Originally published on The Palestine Chronicle The Trump administration, in collusion with scores of public and private colleges and universities, has unleashed one of the most widespread and coordinated campaigns to suppress free speech and restrict the right to protest in US history. The targets? People who have the courage to support Palestinian liberation and sovereignty and to condemn the Israeli government’s genocide in Gaza and its atrocities in the West Bank. While we have seen many attacks on constitutionally protected civil liberties throughout American history, the scope and scale of the systemic repression of Palestinian speech makes this one of the worst. And it’s far from over. The history of the United States has been stained by repeated episodes in which the government, aided and abetted by private organizations and institutions, has deliberately censored speech and punished protests that espouse political views at odds with those in power. While the direct victims of such systemic repression suffer the most, the American people as a whole are also being victimized. Related: Truth Is a Complete Defense: Zohran Mamdani Did Not Defame World Jewry by Condemning Israel’s Genocide in Gaza We are being denied exposure to facts and perspectives which, if freely available, would drive our opposition to policies that the Trump administration, the Israeli government, and their henchmen would prefer go unchallenged. Repression skews public debate in one direction, insulating government propaganda from scrutiny and thereby marginalizing, if not eliminating, inconvenient information and contrary positions. Yet, in tandem, a very different American tradition has taken hold. As brave defenders of the Palestinian people and outspoken critics of Israel are being punished for nothing more than expressing their political views, they and their allies are fighting back, exposing the injustices and organizing nationwide resistance. Indeed, time and again we have seen that the cruel and unjust acts of repression at the hands of the American government and its compliant enablers are eventually exposed by the people themselves, thereby strengthening our resolve to resist and redoubling our demands for justice. Weaponizing Civil Rights Law to Silence Palestine Advocacy Recently, the vast scope of the campaign of repression against Palestinian free speech has been documented in detail in two separate reports from well-recognized defenders of First Amendment rights. Last November, the American Association of University Professors (AAUP) and the Middle East Studies Association (MESA) released a 40-page report entitled ‘Discriminating Against Dissent: The Weaponization of Civil Rights Law to Repress Campus Speech on Palestine’. And in September of this year, the ACLU released a comprehensive 322-page report entitled ‘Student Speech Under Attack: Suppression of Pro-Palestine Speech and Dissent on Campus’. Related: Where Fighting Antisemitism Ends and Censorship Begins The AAUP and MESA report documented how, over the past two years, “the United States government has taken unprecedented steps to suppress campus speech – including scholarship, advocacy, and protest – opposing the state of Israel’s genocidal war against the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip,” thereby paving “the way for profound transformations in U.S. colleges and universities.” The latest suppression goes far beyond the longstanding “Palestine exception” to the First Amendment. “Palestine is less an exception to academic freedom than it is a pretext for erasing the norm altogether, as part of an authoritarian assault on the autonomy of higher education and on the very idea of racial and gender equity.” Counterintuitively, the AAUP and MESA report found that “the most important legal tool of repression against campus speech has been civil rights law – specifically, Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act, which prohibits institutions that receive federal financial assistance from engaging in discrimination on the basis of ‘race, color, or national origin.’ Over the past two decades, pro-Israel actors inside and outside the government have pushed for a reinterpretation of Title VI to include a broad notion of antisemitism that can be easily used to recast many criticisms of Israel as unlawful discrimination. Since late 2023, according to the report, “pro-Israel groups have flooded school administrators and the federal government with claims of antisemitism, which have prompted a wave of investigations; in parallel, these organizations have filed numerous private lawsuits in federal court.” Under pressure from pro-Israel groups, “the Biden administration took steps to advance the conflation of antisemitism and anti-Zionism and thereby rubber-stamped universities’ crackdown on critics.” And the Trump administration “has gone even further, weaponizing antisemitism as a pretext to advance broader far right agendas in higher education.” AAUP and MESA found that all but one of the 102 so-called “antisemitism” complaint letters focus on speech critical of Israel; of these, 79% contain allegations of antisemitism that simply describe criticisms of Israel or Zionism with no reference to Jews or Judaism; and at least 50% of complaints consist solely of such criticism. According to the report, to date, no antisemitism Title VI lawsuits have proceeded to trial or resulted in a judgment for plaintiffs, while Title VI allegations have been dismissed in nine lawsuits, two of which are currently on appeal. While reasons for dismissal have varied, “judges have in some cases exhibited skepticism toward the weaponization of antisemitism claims and raised concerns about First Amendment protections.” In the only appellate decision so far, the First Circuit Court of Appeals declined to characterize Palestine protests at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology as antisemitic harassment, rejecting attempts “to stifle anti-Zionist speech by labeling it inherently antisemitic.” Related: A Hawaii Justice Puts the Roberts Court on Trial “However noble the objective of nondiscrimination, institutions cannot be threatened with civil liability for declining to censor First Amendment protected speech,” noted US District Court Judge Gerald Austin McHugh in rejecting Title VI claims against Haverford College. “Title VI is not a portal for students … to advance their view of how contentious issues should be handled on campus.” In dismissing an antisemitism lawsuit against the University of Pennsylvania, Judge Mitchell Goldberg noted that allegations, “even when read in the most favorable light, could (not) be interpreted as antisemitic …; at worst, Plaintiffs accuse Penn of tolerating and permitting the expression of viewpoints which differ from their own.” Campus Repression and the Cost of Dissent In its report, the ACLU found what could easily be called an unholy alliance of repression between the Trump administration and American colleges and universities. Based on its two-year investigation covering events at 46 public and 34 private university and college campuses located in 28 states and the District of Columbia, the ACLU documented “the heavy-handed and excessive responses by some university and college administrators and police to campus protests concerning Israel’s assault on Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on October 7, 2023.” According to the organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), more than 1,360 student demonstrations took place in the United States between October 7, 2023, and May 3, 2024, protesting the Israeli government’s ongoing military campaign against Palestinians in Gaza and calling for university divestment from Israel and support of Palestinian rights. More than 170 encampments were established in the first semester of 2024. ACLED found that 97 percent of those protests remained peaceful. Indeed, in the more than 10,000 pro-Palestine actions nationwide between October 7, 2023, and May 10, 2024, Crowd Counting Consortium identified property damage at only 128 and police injuries at 13. The vast majority of the instances of property damage involved graffiti or similar defacement of property, and virtually all of the police injuries occurred while making arrests. On campuses, the incidence of property damage was only 30 and police injuries 6. In some cases, students, faculty, and staff engaged in acts of civil disobedience, such as occupying campus buildings, graffitiing, and disrupting classes, as a form of protest. Civil disobedience is part of a long and honorable tradition in America and throughout the world. Henry David Thoreau, Mahatma Gandhi, British suffragettes, Rosa Parks, Nelson Mandela, Occupy Wall Street, and Black Lives Matter come to mind. The American philosopher John Rawls defined civil disobedience as a “public, nonviolent, conscientious yet political act contrary to law usually done with the aim of bringing about a change in the law or policies of the government.” Related: UCLA 9/11 Symposium Sparks Battle Over Academic Freedom The German philosopher Jürgen Habermas argued that in a mature democracy, since protesters who engage in civil disobedience are motivated by a social conscience rather than personal gain, they should be treated leniently, with only nominal punishments or even dismissal of the charges. That’s not what is happening to pro-Palestinian protesters. Overall, the ACLU documented “suppression and retaliation against pro-Palestine speech and expression on campus that began in late 2023 and continues today,” in which colleges and universities “violated basic free speech, association, and assembly rights and caused serious harm when they summoned campus police and local law enforcement, resulting in arrests and unlawful and unnecessary use of force.” Colleges and universities “imposed sweeping restrictions on student speech, initiated disciplinary actions against students, and imposed severe punishments including expulsions and suspensions.” The ACLU found that thousands of protesters have been arrested and disciplined by their schools. In 2024, protesters were detained at more than 70 schools in at least 30 states, according to data collected by The New York Times. More than 3,200 people were arrested by police on university campuses, including students, teachers, human rights observers, and journalists, in many instances for “trespassing.” Students and faculty who participated in Palestine solidarity actions were also subject to doxxing, profiling, and retaliatory attacks by third parties, with little to no protection from their universities and colleges. Since the initial encampment movement, from late 2024 through to publication of the ACLU report in fall 2026, colleges and universities have censored pro-Palestinian expression; punitively enforced campus policies through internal disciplinary or code of conduct processes against students; punished them with suspensions, expulsions, and other sanctions; conducted ongoing surveillance of their activities; and made restrictive changes to school policies governing peaceful assemblies and free speech on campus. The ACLU found that universities have “punitively enforced campus policies through internal disciplinary or code of conduct processes against students, faculty, and staff for campus-related Palestine advocacy.” Hundreds of students have faced sanctions such as campus bans, suspensions, and expulsions for alleged code of conduct violations or disciplinary charges related to their participation in pro-Palestinian demonstrations. These punishments can impose severe and lifelong consequences and profoundly disrupt students’ lives and academic careers. Universities have swiftly imposed interim suspensions and campus bans on students who have been merely arrested or charged with violating campus codes of conduct, before they have been convicted of any crime, the disciplinary process has concluded, or, in some cases, internal investigations have even begun. Hundreds, if not thousands, of students at universities nationwide have faced campus disciplinary proceedings for alleged code of conduct violations carrying potential sanctions. Palestine Legal reported in 2024 that it received 580 requests, and in 2025, 663 requests for legal assistance in cases in which university administrations had launched investigations or imposed sanctions for campus-related Palestine advocacy. The most common punishments students faced in 2025 were interim suspensions and campus bans. Related: Stephen Rohde Accepts Rev. George Regas Courageous Peacemaker Award, Presented by Mike Farrell In some cases, public universities have expelled students for engaging in protected political speech. In other cases, in demonstrations, off-campus protests, and graduation speeches that led to disciplinary actions, the students’ speech was constitutionally protected, and the institutions themselves violated their own student conduct rules and laws. The repression of Palestinian speech on American campuses occurred in partnership with the Trump administration’s vicious crackdown on student activism. The ACLU documents “the Trump administration’s widespread, McCarthyite censorship and retaliation campaign deployed against pro-Palestine advocates on university and college campuses, and against universities that were sites of pro-Palestine student activism.” The administration “abused civil rights laws to suppress criticism of Israel, withhold federal research grants from universities due to their refusal to conform to the government’s preferred ideological approach, and coerce universities into accepting broad-ranging agreements to restore federal funding in exchange for making institutional changes in programs, curricula, admissions, and hiring, curtailing the free speech rights of students and faculty.” The Trump administration also “targeted noncitizen students and scholars for arrest, detention, and deportation based on their political views and in direct retaliation for their advocacy for Palestinian rights.” All told, the ACLU concludes that these repressive measures “have profoundly chilled student speech and advocacy, resulting in a steep decline in protests and a less visible protest movement on campuses across the country.” Fears of “punishment, retribution, or deportation have deterred students and faculty from criticizing Israel or advocating for Palestinian rights.” With over 100 years of experience litigating constitutional law, the ACLU finds that the Trump administration’s actions “violate foundational academic freedom principles, First Amendment rights, and the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly, expression, and association enshrined in international law.” Free Speech and the American Tradition of Resistance In 1860, former slave and eloquent abolitionist Frederick Douglass spoke words on behalf of his enslaved brothers and sisters that reverberate today on behalf of the Palestinian people: No right was deemed by the fathers of the Government more sacred than the right of speech. It was in their eyes, as in the eyes of all thoughtful men, the great moral renovator of society and government. (…) Liberty is meaningless where the right to utter one’s thoughts and opinions has ceased to exist. That, of all rights, is the dread of tyrants. It is the right which they first of all strike down. They know its power. Thrones, dominions, principalities, and powers, founded in injustice and wrong, are sure to tremble, if men are allowed to reason of righteousness, temperance, and of a judgment to come in their presence. Slavery cannot tolerate free speech. Five years of its exercise would banish the auction block and break every chain in the South. They will have none of it there, for they have the power. But shall it be so here? Shall it be so today? Shall it be that the sacred right of Palestinians to freely utter their thoughts and opinions in defense of their liberation and sovereignty will be the great moral renovator of society and government? Only if we, their allies, make it so by organizing, mobilizing, resisting, and voting to banish from power the repressive forces in government, at our colleges and universities, and in every corner of society who cannot tolerate robust, wide-open, and uninhibited free speech protected by the First Amendment. The Palestine Chronicle

articles.title: Colombia Threatens Its Caribbean Neighbor
articles.author: Becca Renk Foster, John Perry
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. When Abelardo de la Espriella was declared the winner of Colombia’s presidential elections, he announced his plan to sever diplomatic relations with Nicaragua, saying, “In my government there will be no ties whatsoever with tyrannies.” In October, he followed this by reviving a longstanding maritime dispute with Nicaragua relating to the San Andrés archipelago in the Caribbean, which had been resolved by the International Court of Justice in 2012 in a judgment repeated just three years ago. “The 2012 ruling seeks to tear apart the archipelago – which is an inseparable whole – and leave our islands as enclaves separated by a foreign sea,” wrote Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara in a post on X on 20 October. Caribbean communities with a shared history The two main islands at the heart of this issue – San Andrés and the smaller Providencia – are considered Colombian territory but are over 400 miles from its mainland. They are, however, just 120 miles from the Nicaraguan coast, and only 95 miles from its closest territory, the Corn Islands. This whole part of the Caribbean has a shared history and culture . Both on the Nicaraguan mainland and across the different islands, the original language is English-based Caribbean Creole, a result of their shared histories of British settlement and enslavement. Protestantism, particularly through Baptist and Moravian churches, is another important influence. The communities share strong Afro-Caribbean food traditions, music and cultural practices. The Raizal people in the San Andrés islands and Nicaragua’s Creole people have each struggled to maintain their Indigenous identities. In the case of Nicaragua, Indigenous identities were recognized by its revolutionary government via its system of autonomous assemblies for the Caribbean regions. However, many Raizals are reported to believe their traditional relationship with the sea has been neglected by the Colombian state and that they were not properly consulted about a dispute that directly affects their livelihoods. Related: The Nicaragua Deportation Story U.S. Media Failed to Investigate The history: a disputed outcome of independence from Spain By the time both Nicaragua and Colombia gained independence from Spain in 1821, the region’s ties to Britain lay in the past, but strong cultural influences remained. Both countries claimed San Andrés and Providencia and other small islands – in Nicaragua’s case because of their proximity, and in Colombia’s because under Spanish rule they had been assigned to New Granada, Colombia’s colonial predecessor. A 1928 treaty appeared to resolve the disputed claims in Colombia’s favor, but the issue has come up many times in the intervening years. It was first reopened after Nicaragua’s 1979 revolution, on the grounds that the treaty had been signed and the islands conceded when Nicaragua was under occupation by the US military. While the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled in 2007 that the islands belonged to Colombia, in 2012 it went on to award substantial maritime rights to Nicaragua (see map). The Court denied Nicaragua’s claim to a wider continental shelf and reiterated this judgment in 2023 when Nicaragua challenged the 2012 ruling. In 2022 the ICJ ruled that Colombia had violated Nicaragua’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the maritime zone by “interfering” with fishing, research, and naval vessels. The 2012 maritime boundary remains the final ICJ judgment binding on both states, and the Court has acknowledged Nicaragua’s willingness to agree fishing rights for the islanders in seas it now controls. Source: International Court of Justice via Wikipedia Commons. The new threat from Colombia’s president It is those wider maritime rights that are now being challenged by President de la Espriella. He dismissed the 2012 ruling during his recent visit and announced plans to redraw Colombia’s nautical map. There is important context to his action. Under de la Espriella’s far-right government, Colombia is now part of the “Shield of the Americas,” a group of countries subservient to the United States, organized to push the “Donroe Doctrine” of complete U.S. dominance in the region. While it has broken diplomatic relations with Nicaragua and Cuba, it has restored ties to Israel . In August, De la Espriella’s government was rewarded by a new, $1 billion security-assistance package from the U.S. State Department. De la Espriella’s threats are particularly dangerous given that the Trump administration has equated narcotrafficking with terrorism, undertaking over 70 attacks on vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific since September 2025 under its so-called “Operation Southern Spear.” Many of the attacks, which have so far killed at least 238 people , are against fishing boats or vessels with no proven connection with drug trafficking. While Washington terms its actions “non-international armed conflict” with non-specified gangs and drug cartels, international law specialists disagree . They argue that the U.S. is not in an armed conflict with any criminal gang and point out that international human rights law prohibits lethal strikes outside of armed conflict, making these illegal, extrajudicial killings. Clearly there is concern that attacks on fishing boats in Nicaragua’s nearby maritime waters, now claimed by Colombia, could be “justified” on a similar basis. Related: “Guaranteeing Peace & Security”: Nicaragua’s Tourism Sector Backs Proposed Reforms El Salvador in the “Shield of the Americas” Nicaragua’s fears are augmented by criticisms from another member of the “Shield of the Americas,” El Salvador. Over the past year, El Salvador’s attorney general has posted on social media at least five times about shipments of cocaine intercepted by Salvadoran authorities that allegedly originate in Nicaraguan territory. Each time, Nicaragua’s military responded with press releases categorically rejecting the accusations. Finally, on 8 October, Nicaragua’s Foreign Ministry sent an official communiqué to San Salvador requesting its government share all evidence of these allegations through the proper channels. “Having this information will allow us to assess what occurred responsibly and to provide the appropriate response, with due legal and diplomatic rigor,” the statement read. “The Government of Nicaragua considers that allegations of this nature should be addressed through the timely exchange of information between the competent authorities and established diplomatic channels.” The repetition of these unfounded allegations by Salvadoran authorities suggests an effort by Nicaragua’s northern neighbor to allege a pattern of drug trafficking which could be used to justify actions against Nicaragua, perhaps by both El Salvador and Colombia. Escalation of conflict But what happens if Colombia unilaterally redraws its maritime boundaries and attacks Nicaraguan fishing boats or a navy vessel in waters that the World Court considers belong to Nicaragua? If Colombia or the U.S. were to carry out military operations in Nicaragua’s territorial waters without its consent, an international armed conflict could be triggered. This would be a bizarrely unequal contest. Whilst Nicaragua spends less on defense than almost every other Latin American country, Colombia has invested in a sizeable navy, with almost ten times as many vessels as Nicaragua’s. Especially if Colombia were to receive US military support, it’s obvious that Nicaraguans at sea would be at severe risk, whether they were undertaking naval patrols or were simply fishing in territorial waters. During his visit to San Andrés , de la Espriella seemed to relish the thought of such a conflict. “Anyone who wants to break the law in Colombia’s waters will find the national navy ready to defend our sovereignty,” he threatened. Raizal fisherfolk visit their counterparts in Nicaragua in 2014. Photo: The Archipielago Press. Related: Is Nicaragua Next? Rubio, the OAS and Washington’s Regime-Change Pressure “Good Living” endangered Fisherfolk from both Nicaragua and Colombia depend on access to these waters not only for their families’ survival but also as an integral part of their cultural identity. Raizal fishermen, in particular, have called for closer relations between the two countries. After the 2012 ruling, a delegation from San Andrés visited Nicaragua to strengthen Indigenous ties. “Intercultural coexistence, combined with physical infrastructure, is what helps us transform the Caribbean Coast into the paradise it is meant to be—a place where Indigenous peoples, Afro-descendants, and mestizos can live, love, and dance together in intercultural harmony,” said Nicaraguan National Assemblyman Johnny Hodgson in an address at the Bluefields Indian and Caribbean University this past April. “That is what El Buen Vivir, ‘Good Living,’ is all about.” For Caribbean families of both countries, however, Colombia’s challenge to Nicaragua’s established maritime boundaries could easily put El Buen Vivir in jeopardy.

articles.title: Black Voter Dilemma
articles.author: Erin Aubry Kaplan
articles.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. On a recent hot afternoon in the Crenshaw district, at an intimate African-themed community center that dates back to the 1960s, a group of seasoned Black activists and concerned citizens met to discuss the mayoral race in L.A., a showdown between incumbent Karen Bass and challenger Nithya Raman that is now in its final weeks. Bass had been flagging in the polls, and the conversation was about how she might regain momentum at this late date. The unspoken consensus at the meeting was that Bass is Black L.A.’s candidate, reflected in part by the mayor’s endorsements by a long list of noted Black organizations, ministers, elected officials and grassroots leaders. Nonetheless, as the meeting progressed, a bigger question surfaced, almost as a side note: Does Bass deserve Black support? After a pause, a few people acknowledged Bass has not been as attentive to the concerns of Black communities as they’d hoped. The comments hung in the air and then the main discussion resumed. There seemed to be little appetite at this point to try and square any criticism of Bass with the desire to see the city’s first Black female mayor win a second term and, as Bass puts it, finish the job. While people freely acknowledged dissatisfaction, they also wanted to stay the course. Not staying the course has been a frequent theme of this mayoral campaign, painted by Bass detractors as an electorate fed up with the declining quality of life in an impossibly expensive city looking for a new way forward. Media outlets from The New York Times to The Guardian have focused on Bass’ opponent and former ally, Nithya Raman, and the latter’s affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America, raising the prospect that she could replicate in L.A. what Zohran Mamdani did in the New York City mayor’s race last year. Mamdani, who is of Indian descent and Muslim, won by creating a coalition advocating for affordability and services across racial and political lines. Raman, who is also of Indian descent, is trying to do something similar by pitching herself as the candidate attuned to urgent citywide problems that people want addressed, now. The twist is that her opponent is another woman of color whose political agenda mostly overlaps with Raman’s but who is nonetheless lagging in the polls — unusual for an incumbent. That’s the surface story. The deeper narrative — about the racial dynamic that helped put Bass in office four years ago as the city’s first Black and first woman mayor — is less sexy, but still important. Four years ago, with the country still in the tailwinds of the George Floyd racial justice movement, Bass made history by defeating Rick Caruso, the white, wealthy Republican and independent-turned- Democrat businessman and civic figure who outspent her five to one. Though Bass never lagged in the polls, the victory was still seen as David beating Goliath, and a boost for Black equity. The guarded euphoria of Bass’ Black supporters in 2022 has since cooled to staying the course. But that’s typical. Related: Destination Crenshaw: Can a $150 Million Art Project Save Black Los Angeles? Historically, Black people have often had to weigh a full slate of ideals against the reality of a candidate actually fulfilling them; in measuring success they tend to look at percentages, not ideological purity. Bass is no exception. And in 2026, retaining a Black mayor is more than relevant in a city where the Black population is shrinking — down to about 8% today from a peak of 18% in 1970 — and losing local representation. Case in point is the race for a City Council seat in the 9th district in South L.A., a longstanding Black electoral stronghold that will not have a Black councilmember for the first time in more than 60 years. In that sense Bass looms even larger now than she did four years ago. At the same time, Bass, by virtue of being mayor, has become part of a larger fight against the anti-blackness of Donald Trump, who has continually disparaged Black Democrats and the cities they lead, Black women and California leaders and elected officials in particular. Bass checks all three boxes, not to mention she represents the largest number of constituents among all Black-led cities in the country. So overt is this denigration that Trump recently suggested, less than half-jokingly, that if Iran wanted to attack the U.S., “They can take out a city. Let them take out L.A. Let them take out San Diego.” (Though he walked back the comments later, it was hardly a mea culpa.) The recent Justice Department raid of the home of Somali-American U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar of Minnesota speaks volumes about the contempt in which Trump holds Black women, especially those in elected office who dare to criticize him. He has repeatedly insulted Omar’s African heritage, last year calling Somali Americans “garbage .” It’s part of a pattern of Trump impugning high-profile Black women he sees as enemies, from Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook to Fulton County, Georgia, D.A. Fani Willis. Vice President J.D. Vance recently said that Angie Nixon, a Black Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Florida, is a radical who should leave the country because “she doesn’t belong in America.” Related: We Had Been Friends for 50 Years. Then We Had to Talk About Trump. Things didn’t start off this way . Back in 2023, new mayor Bass told PBS that she had decided to run after seeing up close the devastation of the crack epidemic of the 1990s. She said she wanted to head off another growing Black-centered crisis — homelessness — that would be criminalized instead of treated as a problem to be solved. She worried about normalizing the fact that Black people were a third of unhoused people in Los Angeles despite being less than 10% of its population, and pointed out factors contributing to that statistic, such as the staggering loss of Black wealth during the home ownership meltdown of the Great Recession. And then the political picture changed drastically. In 2023, the Biden administration was interested in helping to address homelessness; since Trump’s return, the GOP has moved in the opposite direction by normalizing, if not actually criminalizing, homelessness — exactly what Bass feared. An executive order in July 2025 replaced Biden’s expansive approach with a vision of quashing homelessness by “ Ending Crime and Disorder on America’s Streets .” While many Black Angelenos think Bass has been unfairly blamed for problems and events beyond her control, notably the Palisades fire, there is nonetheless discontent about what’s seen as her executive inefficiency and her inability to carry out priorities. “Management and oversight has been a complete failure,” said Mike Guynn, a longtime South Central resident and board member of the L.A. chapter of the New Frontier Democratic Club, a Black Democratic organization. “Not enough structure and controls.” He also thinks her initial push for big social change around homelessness, though admirable, was unrealistic. “She had a vision, but she got so consumed with it she neglected other things,” he said. As for Raman, Guynn believes she offers an alternative but “talks too much about what Karen hasn’t done” while being guilty of neglecting her own council responsibilities. Beyond that dissatisfaction, concern over the larger picture of anti-Blackness in the country and Bass’ role in standing up to it may be why Black voters don’t appear to be shifting, at least in any public or vocal way, in great numbers toward Nithya Raman. Recent polling shows Raman has gained significant support from Latinos, but public polling on the views of Black Angelenos has been scarce, making it hard to tell which candidate might be successful in building the kind of multicultural coalition that propelled Mamdani to victory in New York. On Sunday, Raman announced her endorsement by the Black Los Angeles Young Democrats and the release of her campaign’s Black agenda that promises to address gentrification and bolster Black businesses, among other things. It comes in the aftermath of controversial remarks Raman made during a recent mayoral debate about former police chief Daryl Gates, whom she credited with instituting “the gold standard in terms of noncooperation with immigration enforcement.” Anger erupted among many Black leaders who see Gates’ legacy as one of entrenched racist policing that ultimately failed the city. Raman later apologized . Related: Connie Rice: You Can’t Fight for Racial Justice in a Tyranny It’s useful to remember that L.A. and New York, though similarly diverse, are not the same place and that building durable coalitions here is tough, sometimes unrewarding work that requires patience. As Jim Newton recently observed in a CalMatters opinion piece, Bass does well with older migrant communities — communities that Councilman Marqueece Harris-Dawson says includes Black folks who migrated here from the South who equated L.A. and its promise of single family homes and more personal freedoms with what the piece described as “liberty itself.” In contrast, Raman does better with younger people, many of whom are newer arrivals (this includes Raman, who moved here in 2013) who don’t mind denser housing and who aren’t wedded to more traditional concepts of the California Dream. But ethnic constituencies in L.A. do matter, and no one seems more aware of this than Bass. While those constituencies can become a political coalition, as the Black and Jewish communities did in the ’60s and ’70s during Tom Bradley’s heyday, they can also fray over time. At a candidate interview last month sponsored by Jewish groups in the San Fernando Valley, Bass declared, “I will always protect the Jewish community.” Last summer, she stood up for embattled Latino immigrants during the ICE invasions. While in tackling homelessness she has taken on an entrenched problem that disproportionately affects Angelenos who are Black, some observers say Bass has not been as present in Black communities as she has been in others — ironic considering that she began her coalition-building career as an organizer in the early 1990s in the heart of what was then very Black South Central L.A. Observers also point to Bass’ and Raman’s divergent views on political issues that go beyond Los Angeles but are increasingly important to Black voters , like Israel and Palestine. At the Valley event, Raman stood firm in calling Israel’s war in Gaza a genocide, while Bass rejected the term. Still, it remains unclear whether Raman and her supporters have built the kind of multiethnic coalition necessary to win. Black ties with the Democratic Socialists of America actually go back decades. Co-founder Michael Harrington met Martin Luther King Jr. in the 1960s, as King was moving closer to outright socialism in his calls for poor people of all colors to prioritize domestic spending over war. Harrington, author of The Other America — a popular treatise on the poor — advised King on his Poor People’s Campaign, the last and most ambitious campaign of King’s life. But maybe embracing socialism isn’t really a useful way to gauge the desire for change among people of color. In its analysis of New York City’s 2025 mayoral election, the Manhattan Institute noted that “Mamdani’s large margins with Latino and Black New Yorkers do not make those communities ‘socialist’. Rather, their support signals a profound alienation from local politics, a sense of being unheard on issues such as rent, wages, transit and groceries.” Guynn, with the New Frontier Democratic Club, points to one big-picture reality that doesn’t work in Bass’ favor: The 73-year-old mayor is part of the ongoing struggle among Democrats to reinvent the party at a watershed moment. “Karen has her own progressive ways, but she’s still entrenched with the old Democratic Party,” Guynn said. “She represents the problem with the party at large — caught between what it needs to be now and what it’s traditionally been.” Related: LAPD Shot Her Dog—and America Finally Saw a Black Woman’s Pain That problem is most critical for Black people, the backbone of the party who’ve had to watch Democrats’ mostly ineffectual response to the GOP’s open assault on diversity and civil rights. Guynn expects a victory for Bass nonetheless, though with a small ‘v.’ “She’ll pull it off, but it won’t be a mandate,” he said. Not the stuff of euphoria. But nobody, especially Black Angelenos, expects that anymore. Capital & Main
